paragraphs.text: This verse speaks of Solomon's plea that God would come to dwell in His house and bless it, and settle and rest in it through the ark of His covenant, which proclaims the power of God (His might) and His greatness above all gods.

As the priests stand before God, they are clothed not with linen garments but with righteousness and salvation, that is, purity from every evil, as befits being in the presence of God. Then all the pious people rejoice at God's condescension and His presence in their midst. The effect of these verses may be clearer still in the New Testament, when the priests are present before the Body and Blood of the Lord in the Divine Liturgy, and the priests together with the people receive salvation through the Holy Sacraments and all rejoice.

Solomon also pleads with God not to turn away from His temple and from His anointed, that is, Solomon, anointed by God as king, because of any weakness or sin into which he or his people may fall, but to bear with them, embrace them and forgive them. This is a beautiful humility on Solomon's part before God.

And as Solomon feels his own weakness, he pleads for God's mercies for the sake of the godliness of his father David, as God promised his father mercy for him and for his offspring if they obeyed His commandments.

Be humble before God and you will obtain His mercies, knowing that everything in which you excel is a grace from Him and not from yourself. Then God will bless you and add new blessings to you, as long as you give thanks with humility. The celebration of the Temple, the descent of the fire and the appearance of God

In this verse we see that after Solomon finished his prayer, fire came down from heaven and consumed the burnt offering and the sacrifices offered on the bronze altar, and in this way the glory of God appeared mightily in His temple. This fire means the following:
1- God's acceptance of the sacrifices of Solomon and his people.
2- God's pleasure with Solomon and His agreement to answer his petitions.
3- God's pleasure with the house that Solomon built and His agreement to dwell in it.
4- The fear of God, for our God is a consuming fire. A great fear came upon the priests and the Levites, and they went out of the temple, as will appear in (v. 2).

5- The fire burns up sin and purifies us from it, because the burnt offerings and the sacrifices are a type of Christ, who bore our sins on the Cross and endured their punishment, that is, death, on our behalf.

6- The fire is a symbol of the descent of the Holy Spirit in the New Testament on the day of Pentecost upon the Apostles gathered in the upper room, in the form of tongues of fire, and He founded the Church.

The priests felt the fear of God and could not stand inside the house of the Lord, since they could not bear the majesty of His presence. Thus we saw the appearance of God in (ch. 5:14) in the form of a thick cloud; here He appears in the form of fire coming down from heaven; and then, a little later in this chapter (v. 12), by a clear voice heard by Solomon.
Variegated: containing the two colors, white and black.

The people saw God's descent in the form of the heavenly fire and the priests going out of the temple, so they all bowed down in reverence before the majesty of God, and then praised Him and thanked Him for His condescension and for dwelling in His house in their midst. And they blessed God because He is good and merciful forever, as they had learned from David the prophet (Ps 118:1).

Praising God lifts your heart to heaven, so you cling to God and contemplate His beauty and majesty, and your sins and worldly desires fall away from you. Then you are enlightened and feel God in your life, and you live and rejoice with Him.

entries.section: (2) Rehoboam fortifies the cities of his kingdom and arms them

paragraphs.text: Cities for defense: fortified cities, which hold out if enemies besiege them.

Rehoboam settled in the city of Jerusalem, the capital of his kingdom, which was called Judah and included the tribes of Judah and Benjamin, because they adjoin each other. And he took care to fortify many cities in his kingdom, so that they would be strong and equipped, and would not be affected if enemies besieged them, and would be hard to storm.

entries.section: (2) Rehoboam fortifies the cities of his kingdom and arms them

paragraphs.text: Bethlehem: a city lying south of Jerusalem, about five miles away. It is in a fortified position, because it is on the slope of a mountain, and in it were born David and his offspring, that is, Christ.
Etam: a village lying near Bethlehem, seven miles south of Jerusalem.
Tekoa: a city lying on a mountain in a desolate, empty region, ten miles south of Jerusalem and five miles south of Bethlehem.
Beth-zur: it lies in the mountains of Judah, 4.5 miles north of Hebron.
Shoco: it lies in the plain of Judah, fourteen miles southwest of Bethlehem.
Adullam: twenty miles southwest of Jerusalem.
Gath: one of the five great cities of the Philistines, captured by David (1 Chr 18:1); it lies southwest of Jerusalem.
Mareshah: it lies in a plain, southwest of Jerusalem.
Ziph: it lies in a mountainous region, south of Hebron, four miles away.
Adoraim: it lies west of Hebron, five miles away.
Lachish: a fortified city lying southwest of Jerusalem, forty miles away, on the road to Gaza that leads to Egypt.
Azekah: a city lying near Adullam and Shoco, about twenty miles south of Jerusalem.
Zorah: a city in the plain of Judah, lying southwest of Jerusalem, next to the tribe of Dan.
Aijalon: it lies west of Jerusalem, fourteen miles away, near the tribe of Dan.

Hebron: it lies southwest of Jerusalem, eighteen miles away, and is now called the city of Hebron (al-Khalil). Rehoboam fortified fifteen cities, all lying south and west of Jerusalem, to face the Egyptian invasions. But soon afterwards Shishak king of Egypt attacked the kingdom of Judah, and these cities could not protect the kingdom of Judah, because reliance on God is the true protection, as the Psalm says: "Except the Lord keep the city, the watchman waketh but in vain" (Ps 127:1).
Rely on God, do your duty, and trust that He is able to protect you, whatever dangers or threats surround you, for He is a fortress for everyone who takes refuge in Him.

entries.section: (2) Rehoboam fortifies the cities of his kingdom and arms them

paragraphs.text: Rehoboam appointed strong captains as chiefs over these cities, and appointed for them storehouses of food, oil and wine, so that they would not lack the basic necessities of life, however long the siege.

entries.section: (2) Rehoboam fortifies the cities of his kingdom and arms them

paragraphs.text: Shields: plural of shield, which is a piece of wood covered with leather and having a handle at the back, in which the warrior puts his hand and moves it, to protect his head and body from the enemy's arrows.
Rehoboam also took care to arm these cities so that they would resist the enemy, so he put in them defensive weapons, such as shields, and offensive weapons, such as spears.
And in this Rehoboam felt secure and in possession of the tribe of Judah, which includes a vast area of land, and the small tribe of Benjamin, which lies east of Judah and adjoins it.

entries.section: (3) The priests, the Levites and the devout from the tribes come to Jerusalem

paragraphs.text: The he-goats: male goats. The ancient Egyptians believed that demons dwelt in them, so they worshiped he-goats out of fear of them, and Jeroboam, who had lived for a time in Egypt, took this worship from them and established it among the tribes.
Their suburbs: the open spaces surrounding the cities of the Levites, in which their flocks grazed.

After the kingdom was split and the tribes were divided under the leadership of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, the latter set up calves in Bethel and Dan, and commanded his people to worship them and also to worship he-goats. The priests and the Levites refused the worship and service of idols, and came to Jerusalem to serve the Lord in His temple, leaving their possessions. As for Jeroboam, he appointed priests for the idols who were not of the offspring of Aaron (1 Kgs 12:31).

entries.section: (3) The priests, the Levites and the devout from the tribes come to Jerusalem

paragraphs.text: The believers among the people of God who held fast to His worship could not accept the worship of idols that Jeroboam imposed, and they followed the example of the priests and the Levites, so they left their land and came to Jerusalem, in order to remain steadfast in the worship of God.

May your goal in life be clear, namely preparation for the Kingdom, so that you give priority to your relationship with God before all your work and responsibilities. And if anything conflicts with God, give it up, so that you may remain in the enjoyment of fellowship with God.

entries.section: (3) The priests, the Levites and the devout from the tribes come to Jerusalem

paragraphs.text: God warned Rehoboam that the fortifications of his kingdom were not the fortified cities but returning to God and worshiping Him. So when the priests, the Levites and the devout of the children of Israel came to him and established the worship of God faithfully and carefully, King Rehoboam took courage and grew strong, for around him were the faithful from all the tribes praying, and he too turned his heart to God. So his kingdom was established, and he remained so for three years, worshiping God, he and the people in the kingdom of Judah.

Here some of the wives and sons of Rehoboam are mentioned. It mentions his marriage to Mahalath the daughter of Jerimoth the son of David, that is, Mahalath was a granddaughter of David. We notice that Jerimoth is not among the sons of David mentioned previously in the Holy Bible, so he was most likely the son of one of David's concubines.

Rehoboam also married Abihail the daughter of Eliab, David's eldest brother (1 Sam 16:6), and she was most likely a granddaughter of Eliab (a granddaughter is sometimes mentioned as a daughter), and he fathered a number of sons, some of whom are mentioned here. And Rehoboam also married Maachah the daughter of Absalom the son of David, who was a granddaughter of Absalom through his daughter Tamar (2 Sam 14:27) (but, as we said, a granddaughter is in many cases called a daughter), and he fathered by her a number of sons, among them Abijah, whom his father preferred because he loved his mother Maachah more than all his wives; therefore he appointed Abijah to reign after him.

Rehoboam married a great number of women: eighteen wives and sixty concubines. In this he followed the example of his father Solomon, but he loved Maachah more than all his wives. Perhaps his marriage to so many women distracted him from God, so he turned away from Him three years after the beginning of his reign.
But among the good things recorded of Rehoboam is that all his wives were from the tribe of Judah, that is, there were no foreign women among them, as there were in the case of his father Solomon.

Do not be preoccupied with the pleasures of the world, even if you have the right to use them, lest they distract your heart from God, and your falling into sin becomes easy and you move away from the Kingdom of Heaven.
Rehoboam chose the daughter of Abijah to succeed him on the throne of the kingdom, either because of distinguished qualities in him, or because he was the son of Maachah, his beloved wife.

entries.section: (1) Rehoboam's apostasy and Shishak's attack on him

paragraphs.text: The events of this verse are recorded in (1 Kgs 14:22-24). Rehoboam did not continue in the worship of God, perhaps under the influence of his Gentile mother Naamah the Ammonitess, so he walked in evil and idolatry, and the sodomites appeared in his kingdom, that is, uncleanness and sexual perversion spread, and the people followed their king in these evils and turned away from God. We notice the abbreviation of the details of the evils in this book compared with the Book of Kings, because here it focuses on the line of salvation in David and his offspring, the kings of Judah, until Christ should come.

And we see that Rehoboam's aim in worshiping God was that his kingdom should be strong, and this was by the support of the priests, the Levites and those of the believers from the tribes who had returned. And when the kingdom was established, that is, when he had secured his strength, he forsook God and betrayed Him by worshiping idols, and then God abandoned him, so the king of Egypt attacked him, as we shall see in the following verses.

entries.section: (1) Rehoboam's apostasy and Shishak's attack on him

paragraphs.text: The events of Shishak's attack are recorded briefly in (1 Kgs 14:25-28), and we see in this verse that Rehoboam walked with God for three years, and in the fourth year he turned away from God and worshiped idols and all the uncleanness connected with them. So God was long-suffering with him for a year, the fourth year, and in the fifth year Shishak king of Egypt attacked him, Egypt being the strongest nation in the world at that time, since it was considered the first empire in the world.
And the Book of Chronicles recorded the details of Shishak's attack to show God's punishment of those who reject Him, that is, to declare that salvation lies in holding fast to the worship of God.

entries.section: (1) Rehoboam's apostasy and Shishak's attack on him

paragraphs.text: Lubims: the inhabitants of Libya.
Sukkiims: the Arabs, inhabitants of the desert and the caves in the mountains, near the Red Sea. Ethiopians (Cushites): giant men renowned in war, who are the inhabitants of Abyssinia.
Shishak attacked with a great army, of countless number, from the Egyptians and the surrounding lands, and with many weapons, for it included twelve hundred chariots and sixty thousand horsemen.

entries.section: (1) Rehoboam's apostasy and Shishak's attack on him

paragraphs.text: Shishak was able to take the fortified cities that Rehoboam had prepared, because there is no power that can stand before the power of God when He wants to discipline His people. Then Shishak reached the capital, Jerusalem.

entries.section: (1) Rehoboam's apostasy and Shishak's attack on him

paragraphs.text: The princes of Judah who were in the cities of Judah were afraid and fled to Jerusalem to take refuge in it, so God sent His prophet Shemaiah a second time; for he had come first to Rehoboam and told him not to fight the tribes that had broken away from him (ch. 11:2-4). And here he came to declare to Rehoboam and his princes that they had forsaken God and worshiped idols; therefore God had abandoned them and left them to be enslaved and humbled by Shishak.
And we notice that Shemaiah was a prophet and a historian, for he wrote the acts of Rehoboam, as appears from (v. 15).

entries.section: (1) Rehoboam's apostasy and Shishak's attack on him

paragraphs.text: When the princes heard God's punishment through Shemaiah the prophet, they humbled themselves before God in prayers, austerity and tears, seeking His mercy. Then Shemaiah was sent to them a third time and informed them that He had accepted their repentance, although it was not complete, that is, not from the whole heart of all the princes and the people; but God in His compassion would prevent Shishak from destroying Jerusalem and killing those in it, giving them an opportunity for deliverance so that they might complete their repentance and their worship of Him. But God allowed the people of the kingdom of Judah to be enslaved, so that they might know the difference between their ease while worshiping God and their humiliation while worshiping the nations, under the hand of Shishak king of Egypt.

entries.section: (1) Rehoboam's apostasy and Shishak's attack on him

paragraphs.text: These verses are recorded in (1 Kgs 14:26-28), and we notice in them Rehoboam's concern for appearance, for he made shields of brass so that he would seem a great king, although he had lost the golden shields and had become poor and humbled before the king of Egypt.

entries.section: (1) Rehoboam's apostasy and Shishak's attack on him

paragraphs.text: We sense here Rehoboam's repentance and his humbling himself before God because of the distress into which he had fallen, namely Shishak's attack. And we see on the other side God's compassion toward him, for He did not allow Shishak to destroy Rehoboam and ruin his whole kingdom, but preserved His holy city Jerusalem and His temple that is in it, and gave life to Rehoboam and his kingdom.

And God saw good things in Judah, so He had compassion on the kingdom and did not destroy it. These good things were perhaps the repentance of some of the believers, the priests and the Levites, who had turned away from the worship of God and been occupied with idols, and the return of some of them to God because of the distress that came upon them from the king of Egypt. And this compassion of God was referred to in (v. 7) through the mouth of Shemaiah, that God rejoiced at the people's repentance when they humbled themselves, and gave them a little deliverance.

May you seize the opportunity of God's compassion, so that you repent while you are in this life and humble yourself before Him when distress comes upon you, instead of complaining. Return to Him, for He loves you and is ready to compensate you for all that you lost because of your sins.

These verses are recorded in (1 Kgs 15:1, 2, 6) and have been explained, but one difference is noticed here: it is mentioned in the First Book of Kings that Abijah was the son of Maachah the daughter of Absalom, whereas here it says that Abijah was the son of Michaiah the daughter of Uriel. The explanation is that Uriel was not a son of Absalom but the husband of Tamar the daughter of Absalom, so Abijah is the son of Michaiah, the granddaughter of Absalom, who is also called Maachah, as mentioned in (ch. 11:20) and (1 Kgs 15:2). We must know that the Hebrew original of the word "granddaughter" itself means "daughter." The conclusion is that Abijah is the son of Michaiah, who is also called Maachah, and she is the daughter of Uriel, the husband of Tamar the daughter of Absalom; so Abijah is the son of Michaiah, or Maachah, the granddaughter of Absalom.

Abijah prepared his army from the kingdom of Judah, and it was four hundred thousand soldiers, while Jeroboam's army was eight hundred thousand soldiers from the tribes, that is, double the army of the kingdom of Judah. But the strength of Abijah and his soldiers lay in their reliance on God and their worship of Him in His holy temple.

Reliance on God is able to sustain you in every situation, however difficult. So take care of your repentance and your relationship with God; then you will live in assurance in the face of the devil's wars.
(2) Abijah's address to the tribes (vv. 4-12)
4- And Abijah stood up upon mount Zemaraim, which is in mount Ephraim, and said, Hear me, thou Jeroboam, and all Israel;

5- Ought ye not to know that the LORD God of Israel gave the kingdom over Israel to David for ever, even to him and to his sons by a covenant of salt? 6- Yet Jeroboam the son of Nebat, the servant of Solomon the son of David, is risen up, and hath rebelled against his lord. 7- And there are gathered unto him vain men, the children of Belial, and have strengthened themselves against Rehoboam the son of Solomon, when Rehoboam was young and tenderhearted, and could not withstand them.

8- And now ye think to withstand the kingdom of the LORD in the hand of the sons of David; and ye be a great multitude, and there are with you golden calves, which Jeroboam made you for gods. 9- Have ye not cast out the priests of the LORD, the sons of Aaron, and the Levites, and have made you priests after the manner of the nations of other lands? so that whosoever cometh to consecrate himself with a young bullock and seven rams, the same may be a priest of them that are no gods. 10- But as for us, the LORD is our God, and we have not forsaken him; and the priests, which minister unto the LORD, are the sons of Aaron, and the Levites wait upon their business: 11- And they burn unto the LORD every morning and every evening burnt sacrifices and sweet incense: the shewbread also set they in order upon the pure table; and the candlestick of gold with the lamps thereof, to burn every evening: for we keep the charge of the LORD our God; but ye have forsaken him. 12- And, behold, God himself is with us for our captain, and his priests with sounding trumpets to cry alarm against you. O children of Israel, fight ye not against the LORD God of your fathers; for ye shall not prosper.

Mount Zemaraim: Zemaraim is a city in the portion of Benjamin and on its border (Josh 18:22). When Abijah found that Jeroboam had attacked him with a great army of eight hundred thousand, he prepared the army of Judah, which was four hundred thousand, as we saw in (v. 3), but he did not rush into the war, because Shemaiah the prophet had warned the kingdom of Judah not to fight the kingdom of Israel, that is, the tribes (ch. 11:4). But he tried to stop the war by going up to Mount Zemaraim, which is on the border of his kingdom, and standing to address Jeroboam and his armies drawn up on the border of the two kingdoms. This shows Abijah's courage and his lack of fear that one of the enemies might shoot him with an arrow.
Covenant of salt: salt preserves food, and what is meant by a covenant of salt is a covenant that is not broken or spoiled, that is, a firm covenant.

Abijah began to explain to Jeroboam and his armies the reasons that would make the army of Judah triumph over the army of the tribes, and he gave the first proof, which is that God gave an everlasting, firm covenant to David and his offspring, that they might reign over the children of Israel. Here Abijah means that the kingdom belongs to David and his offspring over all Israel, and that the division that occurred was an anomaly, and it would have been right for the tribes to remain subject to the offspring of David, to whom the covenant belongs.

Young and tenderhearted: a description of Rehoboam meaning that he was weak like the young and tenderhearted, that is, he did not have the strength and firmness of men, although he was forty-one years old when he began to reign (ch. 12:13). Children of Belial: Belial means Satan, and what is meant is the sons of evil.

The second proof of the certainty of Abijah's victory is that Jeroboam was merely a servant of Solomon the son of David, and a rebellious, mutinous servant, who fled to Egypt, then returned in rebellion and gathered wicked men and broke away with the tribes from subjection to the offspring of David, that is, Rehoboam, exploiting his weakness. The meaning of this is that the kingdom belongs to King Abijah, because he is of the offspring of David, and not to the rebellious servant who usurped the kingdom, namely Jeroboam.

The third proof is that the kingdom of Judah is the kingdom of the Lord, in the hand of the offspring of David, that is, King Abijah, whereas the kingdom of Israel relied on the pagan gods, namely the golden calves, and relied on the multitude of their number, which is worthless before the power of the Lord; indeed, their worship of the calves will be a cause of the Lord's vengeance upon them.

Consecrates himself (fills his hand): offers a sacrifice, that is, devotes himself to the priesthood and becomes a priest. The fourth proof is that the kingdom of Judah relied on the worship of God in His temple and on the official priests, who are of the offspring of Aaron, whereas the kingdom of Israel worshiped idols and relied on priests who were not of the offspring of Aaron as God commanded, but any person who offered a sacrifice became a priest, and they drove out the priests of God, who were of the offspring of Aaron.

The fifth proof is the holding fast of the people of the kingdom of Judah to the worship of God in His temple, offering the sacrifices and the offerings, and likewise lighting the lamps and offering incense and sweet spices, that is, offering complete worship to God, and consequently enjoying His care and His unconquerable power.

The sixth proof is that God is the true commander of the armies of the kingdom of Judah, and He is the captain before whose power no one can stand, nor before the shout of His priests with the trumpets. Who can fight against God?! And the priests' shout with the trumpets means the presence of God as the commander of His army.
In the end he gives advice to the tribes of Israel, led by Jeroboam, which is that they should not attack and fight the kingdom of Judah, because they will be defeated.

In the preceding verses Abijah appears in a good light, relying on God and His worship, but in truth he did evil in the sight of the Lord, like Rehoboam his father, and he was not perfect like David (1 Kgs 15:3). But an important question appears: if Abijah walked in evil like Rehoboam, why did God give him victory over Jeroboam? The answer is that God wanted to discipline Jeroboam for his increase in evil, and He used Abijah in that, not because of Abijah's goodness but because Jeroboam's evils were far greater.

And although God did not permit Rehoboam to fight the breakaway tribes (ch. 11:4), He permitted Abijah here to fight the tribes and to triumph over them, because of the multitude of the sins of the kingdom of Israel.

And we notice a contradiction between Abijah's words and his conduct. In his previous address to Jeroboam, he declares that the Lord is his God and that he has not forsaken Him, although at the same time he allowed the worship of idols, and he rebuked Jeroboam for relying on the golden calves while he himself left the people to worship strange gods, and even allowed idols inside his own house, since his mother Maachah worshiped idols. So Abijah took on the form of godliness while denying its power, and God was angry at this, so his reign lasted only three years.

Remember your covenant with God in the sacraments of Baptism and the Holy Myron, and also in the sacraments of confession and Holy Communion, so that you return to God with your heart and walk in what pleases Him, and the devil will not prevail over you.
(3) Abijah's victory over Jeroboam (vv. 13-20)
13- But Jeroboam caused an ambushment to come about behind them: so they were before Judah, and the ambushment was behind them.

14- And when Judah looked back, behold, the battle was before and behind: and they cried unto the LORD, and the priests sounded with the trumpets. 15- Then the men of Judah gave a shout: and as the men of Judah shouted, it came to pass, that God smote Jeroboam and all Israel before Abijah and Judah. 16- And the children of Israel fled before Judah: and God delivered them into their hand. 17- And Abijah and his people slew them with a great slaughter: so there fell down slain of Israel five hundred thousand chosen men. 18- Thus the children of Israel were brought under at that time, and the children of Judah prevailed, because they relied upon the LORD God of their fathers. 19- And Abijah pursued after Jeroboam, and took cities from him, Bethel with the towns thereof, and Jeshanah with the towns thereof, and Ephrain with the towns thereof. 20- Neither did Jeroboam recover strength again in the days of Abijah: and the LORD struck him, and he died.
Ambush: a group of soldiers hidden, who appear at the right time to surprise the enemy. Jeroboam did not heed Abijah's warnings, because he relied on two things:
1- The great number of his soldiers, for they were double the number of the soldiers of the kingdom of Judah.
2- His military skill, for he laid a plan for victory, which was setting an ambush.

Jeroboam moved with his military plan, and attacked Abijah and did not withdraw despite all of Abijah's warnings to him. At the same time he made a group of his soldiers hide, then circle around, perhaps behind one of the mountains, then circle to come behind the army of Judah, so that the army of Judah would be surrounded in front and behind by the armies of Israel, and they would strike it from the front and from behind, and consequently it would be easy for Jeroboam to triumph over them. So Jeroboam thought.

When Abijah found that he was surrounded in front and behind by the armies of Jeroboam, he and all his soldiers cried out to God, on whom they had relied. And the priests sounded the trumpets, to declare that God is the One fighting for Judah, so the soldiers of Judah took courage because of their reliance on God.

When the soldiers of Judah grew strong, they shouted, asking for God's help, and when they shouted God answered their prayers, so He intervened and struck Jeroboam and all his army with a blow that made them weak before the soldiers of Judah. The Holy Bible does not mention this blow specifically; it may have been a disease, or a sudden bodily weakness, as He struck the Arameans in the days of Elisha with blindness (2 Kgs 6:18), or fear and terror in the heart, or any other blow, as God had struck the enemies of His people before with stones (Ezek 38:22) or with hornets (Josh 24:12).

Prayer is very powerful, especially when it comes from a weak person who seeks God's help with all his heart, for He must intervene. Therefore hasten to God with faith, however great your weakness, that He may fight for you against all adverse circumstances.

Abijah was strengthened by the power of God and struck the armies of Jeroboam that were before him and behind him, and killed five hundred thousand of them. Thus Jeroboam was broken, who had tried to subdue and seize the kingdom of Judah relying on his own strength; more than half his army was killed, and he fled in shame before God, the Defender of His children, the people of Judah, who were strengthened when they relied on Him. This is the reward of the believers who relied on their God.

Bethel: it lies north of Jerusalem, twelve miles away, and was considered a holy city because God appeared in it to Jacob (Gen 28:19). Jeshanah: a city in the mountain of Ephraim, lying north of the kingdom of Judah.
Ephrain: a city lying north of Jerusalem, 8 km away.

Abijah continued his victories, so he pursued the armies of Jeroboam and took a number of cities in the south of the kingdom of Israel, that is, near the border of the kingdom of Judah, such as Bethel, Bashan and Ephrain.

Jeroboam lived in shame and humiliation after his defeat before Abijah, and could not attack the kingdom of Judah a second time. Then God struck him with a disease that continued for years until he died, two years after the death of Abijah. (4) Abijah's family (vv. 21, 22)
21- But Abijah waxed mighty, and married fourteen wives, and begat twenty and two sons, and sixteen daughters.
22- And the rest of the acts of Abijah, and his ways, and his sayings, are written in the story of the prophet Iddo.

When Abijah felt his mighty victory over Jeroboam, he became proud, strengthening himself by his own power, and plunged into his desires, so he married fourteen wives and fathered by them twenty-two sons and sixteen daughters. The book does not mention Abijah's sins here, because it is concerned with the plan of salvation, but the Book of Kings tells us that Abijah's heart was not perfect, and despite his good address and his reliance on God, he returned and felt his own strength and relied on himself.
Take care to be humble before God and to thank Him at all times for His gifts, so that the devil does not find an opportunity to enter into you, and use the world without plunging into its desires.
Midrash: a Hebrew word meaning a book in which interpretations and sermons are recorded.
The book tells us here that the details of Abijah's life, his conduct, his words and the meaning they carry were written by Iddo the prophet in a book.
Asa reigns after Abijah

Abijah died after reigning over Judah for three years, and they buried him with the kings before him in the city of David, and then his son Asa reigned in his place (1 Kgs 15:9). He was young, but it seems that he had learned reliance on God through the victory of his father Abijah over Jeroboam (ch. 13), and he followed the example of his forefather David (1 Kgs 15:11), whom he regarded as his father, although the surrounding atmosphere was evil, for his father Abijah and his grandfather Rehoboam had walked in evil for no little time, in addition to the fact that his grandmother Maachah worshiped idols and was a strong, dominating personality. Because of Asa's faith and his attachment to God, God gave him security in his kingdom of Judah and put fear in the heart of Jeroboam after his defeat at the hands of Abijah, so Asa lived ten years at the beginning of his reign in security, which helped him in positive works that will appear in the following verses.

Do not surrender to evil if it surrounds you in the conduct of those around you, but hold fast to your faith and the commandments of God, even if you are alone with God, for God is able to sustain you, bless your life and bring the wrongdoers into subjection before you.

Asa's goodness at the beginning of his reign appears in that he set his aim to please God, so he did what was right and good in His eyes. He did not care to please himself or those around him in order to gain fame or pleasures; therefore Asa is counted among the good kings of the kingdom of Judah.
The groves (poles): plural of pole, a piece of wood planted in the ground and rising high, to declare that this place is for the worship of idols, such as Ashtaroth and Baal.
Asa's goodness appears in the following:
1- Removing the pagan altars, that is, those of the strange gods.

2- Removing the worship of idols set up on the high places, although the First Book of Kings (1 Kgs 14:15) mentions that the high places were not taken away, because Asa had permitted the offering of sacrifices to God on these high places, as Solomon had done, and this is a mistake, because sacrifices are offered only in the temple of God, and offering sacrifices to God on the high places turns with time into sacrifices being offered to idols on these high places.
3- He broke the images of the pagan idols.
4- He removed the groves that the former kings had set up for the worship of idols.
In the days of Abijah, Asa's father, the service in the temple was carried on by the priests and the Levites (ch. 13:

10), but Abijah allowed the worship of idols, and his heart was not perfect before God; therefore after Asa removed the worship of idols, he took care to call the people to worship God and hold fast to His commandments and His law, so that they might remain in life with Him and be rid of the effects of pagan worship and the evils connected with it.

Images of the sun: stones or sheets of brass engraved in the form of the sun, set up on pillars, declaring that this place is for the worship of the sun gods. After Asa removed the high places, the worship of the sun gods and the various places of pagan worship, the kingdom of Judah had rest, since the people worshiped God alone in His temple, so God gave them security and rest from all their enemies.
Bars: wooden boards set up to secure the gates.

Asa seized the opportunity of the kingdom of Judah's rest from the attacks of enemies and took care to fortify the cities with walls, gates and towers. Here Asa's activity and striving appear: he was not lazy because of the rest of the land, but took care to fortify the cities, and God prospered him because of his faithfulness. Asa's reliance was on God, whom he had sought, so He gave the land rest and helped him fortify the cities; that is, he did his part, but his reliance was on God.

And building walls to fortify the cities is a type of man's care to guard his senses and thoughts and fortify them with prayer, meditation and spiritual exercises, against the attacks of the enemy, Satan. We notice here that the rest of the land was an opportunity for constructive work, because true rest is in pleasing God and in positive work, and not only in keeping away from sin and the worship of idols. For when a person removes sins by repentance and God gives him rest and helps him, he strives to acquire the virtues, that is, positive work, and he succeeds in all that he does, because God is with him.

To complete the positive work, Asa took care to arm the army of the kingdom of Judah, for despite the rest of the land he prepared a great army, numbering three hundred thousand from the tribe of Judah, armed with shields and spears, in addition to two hundred and eighty thousand from the tribe of Benjamin, armed with shields and bows for shooting arrows. From this the importance of constant readiness and spiritual vigilance appears, so that the devil may not find an opportunity or a gap to make us fall into sin.
(2) Asa's victory over Zerah (vv. 9-15)-
9- And there came out against them Zerah the Ethiopian with an host of a thousand thousand, and three hundred chariots; and came unto Mareshah.

10- Then Asa went out against him, and they set the battle in array in the valley of Zephathah at Mareshah. 11- And Asa cried unto the LORD his God, and said, LORD, it is nothing with thee to help, whether with many, or with them that have no power: help us, O LORD our God; for we rest on thee, and in thy name we go against this multitude. O LORD, thou art our God; let not man prevail against thee. 12- So the LORD smote the Ethiopians before Asa, and before Judah; and the Ethiopians fled. 13- And Asa and the people that were with him pursued them unto Gerar: and the Ethiopians were overthrown, that they could not recover themselves; for they were destroyed before the LORD, and before his host; and they carried away very much spoil. 14- And they smote all the cities round about Gerar; for the fear of the LORD came upon them: and they spoiled all the cities; for there was exceeding much spoil in them. 15- They smote also the tents of cattle, and carried away sheep and camels in abundance, and returned to Jerusalem.

Zerah the Ethiopian (Cushite): a chief or military commander of the Cushites, that is, the Abyssinians, who migrated to the land of the Arabs, that is, Yemen and Saudi Arabia, as proved by Asa's seizing the tents, sheep and camels of the Arabs in (v. 15); or he may have been an Abyssinian commander in Egypt, subject to King Shishak of the Twenty-Second Dynasty, who gathered a great army of Egyptians and with them mercenaries of the Cushites and Libyans, famous for their strength in war (16:8). Mareshah: a city lying in a plain southwest of Jerusalem.
Valley of Zephathah: a valley next to the city of Mareshah.

Zerah the Cushite attacked with a great army, numbering a million soldiers and armed with many weapons, among them three hundred war chariots, to seize the kingdom of Judah, and he encamped near Mareshah. So Asa went out with an army from the kingdom of Judah and met the army of Zerah in the valley of Zephathah.

Because Asa was a good king, he prayed to God, declaring his faith in Him, that He is able to work with the few as with the many, that is, able to give the small army of Judah victory over the great army of Zerah, and he declared his reliance on God, that is, Asa did not move to meet Zerah except relying on the power of God.
And so Asa's success appeared in this test of faith, because he relied on God and did not fear the power and the multitude of Zerah's army.

The importance of Asa's preparation in the days of peace, which lasted ten years, also appeared here. Satan does not surrender, and although God restrained him for ten years, he renews the attack. And because Asa had become accustomed to prayer in the days of peace, it was easy for him to seek God in the distress of Zerah's attack on him, and God answered him, as He had answered in the days of peace, and he triumphed over Zerah.

And we find Asa's humility clear, for he described himself as having no strength before the multitude of Zerah's army, so his only reliance was on God, although the number of Asa's army was not small, for it was five hundred and eighty thousand warriors, strongly armed, yet he relied on God and not on his army.
And we also find Asa's faith clear, in his feeling that God is his own God, who cannot possibly abandon him, so it mentions that he "called on the Lord his God."
Humility is the shortest way to the tender heart of God, so declare your weakness before Him and ask for His help, and you will be able to overcome all the powers of evil.
Gerar: a city south of Jerusalem, 100 km away.

After the prayer Asa advanced and engaged the army of Zerah, and triumphed over it and killed most of the army, so that the Holy Bible mentions here that no living person was left of it, that is, most of Zerah's soldiers were killed. And Asa pursued the army of Zerah a long distance, about 100 km, to Gerar, killing many of the enemies there and taking their spoil, which was a reward from God to Asa for his faith and for his striving. So we see in Asa the necessity of combining spiritual striving with prayer, that is, striving with grace, so that we may obtain victory and the divine reward.
And God's quickness in answering His children in distress appears clearly, for He rescues them and rewards them.

The army of Zerah tried to take refuge in some of the cities around Gerar, so Asa struck them in order to destroy the army of Zerah. He also struck the tents of the Arabs in the valleys, in which the Cushites tried to take shelter. And he took much spoil from the Arabs and these cities, whether camels, sheep or tents, in addition to all kinds of spoil, and they returned victorious to Jerusalem. Perhaps some of Zerah's army had its home in these tents of the Arabs, and in this way Asa destroyed and wiped them out in their own homeland. Asa's revival (1) Azariah's warnings (vv. 1-7)-

1- And the Spirit of God came upon Azariah the son of Oded: 2- And he went out to meet Asa, and said unto him, Hear ye me, Asa, and all Judah and Benjamin; The LORD is with you, while ye be with him; and if ye seek him, he will be found of you; but if ye forsake him, he will forsake you.

3- Now for a long season Israel hath been without the true God, and without a teaching priest, and without law. 4- But when they in their trouble did turn unto the LORD God of Israel, and sought him, he was found of them. 5- And in those times there was no peace to him that went out, nor to him that came in, but great vexations were upon all the inhabitants of the countries. 6- And nation was destroyed of nation, and city of city: for God did vex them with all adversity. 7- Be ye strong therefore, and let not your hands be weak: for your work shall be rewarded.

The Spirit of God came upon a prophet named Azariah, and upon his father Oded, and commanded them to go to meet Asa and the people of the kingdom of Judah. Here we see the coming of the Holy Spirit in the Old Testament as temporary, to accomplish a divine work, and here it is the declaration of a prophecy and the strengthening of the prophet so that he might face the king and all the people with courage; whereas in the New Testament the Holy Spirit dwells permanently in the believers, through the sacrament of the Holy Myron. And if He came here so that all the speech might be with God's precision, our submission in the New Testament to the Holy Spirit makes our words and our works from God.

Azariah stood and said to Asa and the people of the tribes of Judah and Benjamin that God is with them, on condition that they remain holding fast to Him, but if they turn away from Him, He will abandon them; that is, man's will is necessary for his salvation and for his enjoying God's care.

And we notice the timing that God chose for sending Azariah, namely after His people's victory over Zerah the Cushite, so that they would not be absorbed in the victory and the spoil and become proud and forget God, and the devil attack them and make them fall. The continuance of victory is bound to the continuance of cleaving to God and relying on Him.

Azariah the prophet reminds the people that many days had passed over the children of Israel in which they neglected the worship of God, and their priests and their teachings, and likewise the commandments of God and His law. This was clear in the era of the Judges and recurred at various times, such as the days of King Saul and also the ten tribes when they broke away at the hand of Jeroboam. And the prophet's words apply to any period in which the people of God turn away from Him.
And when the people forsook God, their enemies troubled them, so they cried out to God, who hastened to them and rescued them, declaring that they were His people and under His care.

The people fluctuated between the worship of God and neglecting it, so they lost God's care and, consequently, reassurance and security, and were greatly exposed to the attacks of enemies, in addition to the conflicts and internal problems among the people, so they had no rest or peace; and because of the evils of the people of God, He allowed many nations to rise against them, and they killed many of them and even enslaved and humbled them. That is, God allowed the wicked to trouble His people so that they would repent and return to Him, and not perish.

The summary of the prophecy and its purpose, which Azariah declared to the people, is that they should be strong in the Lord, so as to be rid of evil, do good and worship God, and God would reward them with great rewards in this age and in the age to come.

Hold fast to your spiritual rule and your worship of God, whatever your preoccupations or the problems you are going through. By this you secure God's care and support for you, and He will even fight for you and let you enjoy His fellowship.
(2) Asa's response (vv. 8-19)-

8- And when Asa heard these words, and the prophecy of Oded the prophet, he took courage, and put away the abominable idols out of all the land of Judah and Benjamin, and out of the cities which he had taken from mount Ephraim, and renewed the altar of the LORD, that was before the porch of the LORD.

9- And he gathered all Judah and Benjamin, and the strangers with them out of Ephraim and Manasseh, and out of Simeon: for they fell to him out of Israel in abundance, when they saw that the LORD his God was with him. 10- So they gathered themselves together at Jerusalem in the third month, in the fifteenth year of the reign of Asa. 11- And they offered unto the LORD the same time, of the spoil which they had brought, seven hundred oxen and seven thousand sheep. 12- And they entered into a covenant to seek the LORD God of their fathers with all their heart and with all their soul; 13- That whosoever would not seek the LORD God of Israel should be put to death, whether small or great, whether man or woman. 14- And they sware unto the LORD with a loud voice, and with shouting, and with trumpets, and with cornets. 15- And all Judah rejoiced at the oath: for they had sworn with all their heart, and sought him with their whole desire; and he was found of them: and the LORD gave them rest round about. 16- And also concerning Maachah the mother of Asa the king, he removed her from being queen, because she had made an idol in a grove: and Asa cut down her idol, and stamped it, and burnt it at the brook Kidron. 17- But the high places were not taken away out of Israel: nevertheless the heart of Asa was perfect all his days. 18- And he brought into the house of God the things that his father had dedicated, and that he himself had dedicated, silver, and gold, and vessels.
19- And there was no more war unto the five and thirtieth year of the reign of Asa.

Asa responded quickly to the word of God through the mouth of Oded the prophet and his son Azariah, and removed the pagan altars, which he had begun to remove at the beginning of his reign, whether from the lands of the tribes of Judah and Benjamin, or from the cities he had taken from Israel, which lie north of the kingdom of Judah in the mountain of Ephraim. These may be the cities that his father Abijah had taken (ch. 13:19). This is the first reform in the series of Asa's reforms.

The second of Asa's reforms is the renewal of the altar of the Lord that was before the porch, that is, the court in the temple, and this altar is the bronze altar. Perhaps it had fallen into ruin, or suffered some damage, during the period of neglect of worship in the temple, in the days of Rehoboam and Abijah, a period of thirty-five years (17 years of Rehoboam's reign + 3 years of Abijah's reign + 15 years from the beginning of Asa's reign until this time (v. 10).)

The third reform is the gathering of the believers, not only in the kingdom of Judah but also those in the kingdom of Israel, that is, the ten tribes, who heard of the renewal of the worship of God in His temple, so they left their lands and came to Jerusalem to take part in the worship of God and encouraged their brethren in the kingdom of Judah.

How beautiful it is to look for those who love God, to befriend them, so that you are encouraged by them and encourage them in the worship of God. In addition to this is the importance of your friendship with the saints, who have completed their striving on earth and live in the love of God. All this pushes you great steps forward on the way to the Kingdom.

The fourth reform that Asa carried out is offering worship and love of God in abundance, for Asa and his people did not cling to the spoil they had brought from Zerah the Cushite, but offered from it on God's altar seven hundred oxen and seven thousand sheep. Thus the picture of the intense love that Solomon offered at the dedication of the temple of God is renewed (ch. 7:5).

The fifth reform is making a covenant with God to seek Him with all their heart, that is, not to ask anything from the pagan gods and not to rely on their own strength, and whoever does not seek the Lord and takes refuge in idols is put to death. We notice here the repeated seeking of the Lord by Asa in the Second Book of Chronicles from (ch. 14-16), which contains forty-eight verses, in which the seeking of the Lord is repeated five times, and this shows Asa's care for prayer and taking refuge in God.
And the people swore to God to worship Him and seek Him alone; indeed, they shouted and used the trumpets and the horns, declaring their faith in God and their holding fast to Him.

And they rejoiced greatly at this oath and covenant, because they sought God of their own will with all their hearts, that is, the king did not pressure them in this covenant. This shows God's concern for the human will, so God answered them and they felt His presence with them and His blessing, and He gave them rest from the attacks of enemies and peace in their hearts.

These verses are recorded and were explained in (1 Kgs 15:13-15), and we see in them Asa's sixth reform, which is the removal of Queen Maachah and the destruction of her idol and her grove, for he took care to reform the royal palace, that is, his own house, and we see his holding fast to God more than his concern for his family relationships, "We ought to obey God rather than men" (Acts 5:29). This is great courage, because Maachah was a strong, dominating personality.

Because of Asa's goodness and his reforms, God blessed him, so he spent thirty-five years of his reign in rest, which is a long period that shows God's love for him. Here Asa resembles Solomon his forefather, who took care to build the temple of God, so He gave him rest and subdued the nations to him, as the Holy Bible says, "When a man's ways please the LORD, he maketh even his enemies to be at peace with him" (Prov 16:7). The Holy Bible testifies here that Asa's heart was perfect before God (v. 17), so he is counted among the good kings, but it was not like the heart of David his father (1 Kgs 15:3), for David is the perfect measure of the love of God. Asa walked in the way of David's perfection, but only in part, and David was perfect, yet a man with his faults, such as the sin concerning Uriah the Hittite (2 Sam 12:9) and the numbering of the people (2 Sam 24); he is the best king who appeared on the throne of the children of Israel, for when he sinned he repented, and God forgave him; whereas Asa walked in the ways of perfection but his repentance was not complete, for he listened to Oded and Azariah but did not listen to Hanani the seer (ch. 16). Asa's fall and then his death

When Asa fell into relying on men and forsook God, the Lord sent Hanani the seer to rebuke him, and he said to him: Because you relied on the king of Syria to stop Baasha's attack, instead of relying on God, you have lost something great, namely the escape of the king of Syria from your hand; for God's plan was to subdue him to you, so that you would become one of the strongest nations in the region in which you live. Asa's sin is weakness of faith and doubt in God; he feared Baasha and began to look for someone to support him and took refuge in Syria. And Asa's fear drove him to dig a pit to hide in from the face of Baasha, and Jeremiah the prophet referred to it (Jer 41:9).

Hanani reminded King Asa that God had delivered into his hand the very great army of Zerah, armed with chariots and various weapons, because he relied on God, so he did not care about the strength of the Cushites and the Libyans who were with Zerah. And here is a clear rebuke: Why, Asa, did you go back on your faith and your reliance on God, in which you walked with Zerah, and then abandon it with Baasha?!

Hanani made clear to Asa that God is the searcher of hearts and reins and seeks His children who believe in Him, to strengthen and fortify them before all the afflictions they meet; but because you, Asa, have abandoned your faith, God will punish you by raising wars against you from your enemies.

Sadly, Asa did not submit to the voice of God and repent of his sin; on the contrary, he punished Hanani the seer, who had conveyed God's words to him, and threw him into prison to silence the voice of God, that is, the voice of Hanani. And he troubled the believers in God who supported Hanani and tried to push Asa to repentance, and wronged them instead of thanking them.

Accept the voice of God through the mouth of one who reproves you and do not be annoyed at him because of your pride, for God in His love sent these to you so that you might repent and not perish in eternal torment.
And so we find that Asa fell into a series of sins, which are:
1- Weakness of his faith and his not taking refuge in God.
2- Fear of men, that is, of Baasha.
3- Taking refuge in a pagan king, the king of Syria, instead of God.

4- Paying a bribe to Syria of silver and gold from the house of the Lord, instead of adding to the treasury of the house of the Lord from the spoil he obtained from his victories over his enemies by the power of God, as happened when he triumphed over Zerah and took much spoil from him.
5- He encouraged the king of Syria to commit a sin, which is breaking his covenant with Baasha.

6- He made a pagan king fight his cousins, who are the kingdom of Israel, and in this way his own kingdom also was exposed to danger from the king of Syria, who could break his covenant with him at any time.
7- He refused to submit to God's word through Hanani.
8- He wronged the one who declared the truth to him, namely Hanani, and a number of believers in his kingdom, whom he troubled.

entries.section: (1) The greatness of Jehoshaphat because of his holding fast to the commandments of the Lord

paragraphs.text: After the death of Asa his son Jehoshaphat reigned over the kingdom of Judah, and took care to fortify his kingdom against the kingdom of Israel, because of its deviation from the worship of God and its worship of idols. So he placed an army in the fortified cities of Judah and appointed governors to manage them with strength, and he also appointed governors in the cities that Asa had taken from the kingdom of Israel, situated in the tribe of Ephraim. His intention was not to fight the kingdom of Israel but to protect his kingdom from the evils of Israel.

entries.section: (1) The greatness of Jehoshaphat because of his holding fast to the commandments of the Lord

paragraphs.text: Jehoshaphat relied for his strength on God, so he took care of the worship of God in His temple and held fast to His commandments, like David his father, who was the measure of life with God, and he did not slip into the worship of the pagan gods, the most important of which was the god Baal, or the Baalim, whose worship had spread in the kingdom of Israel.

entries.section: (1) The greatness of Jehoshaphat because of his holding fast to the commandments of the Lord

paragraphs.text: Because of Jehoshaphat's cleaving to the worship of God, God established his kingdom, so peace and stability prevailed, and his people submitted to him and also brought him gifts.

entries.section: (1) The greatness of Jehoshaphat because of his holding fast to the commandments of the Lord

paragraphs.text: Jehoshaphat's reforms did not stop at his worship of God, but he took courage and removed the worship of idols that was carried on at the high places, whether the groves, or the altars, or the idols; and this matter was extremely difficult, because the people had become attached to these evil forms of worship.

And although Asa had removed these forms of worship set up at the high places, and took care to walk in the way of the Lord with exactness, that is, he walked in the way of spiritual perfection, he did not follow the people's conduct closely, so some of them returned to this worship, especially at the end of Asa's life, when he fell ill and refused to take refuge in God and did not listen to God's word through the mouth of Hanani the seer, but imprisoned him.

Your relationship with God is the foundation of your success in all your works and your life. May you make God your only goal, and order your life in a way that does not conflict with His will, and in this way you will succeed in everything to which your hands reach out.

entries.section: (2) His teaching of the Law to the people

paragraphs.text: Jehoshaphat was not content with removing the pagan worship at the high places, but also took care of the religious instruction of his people, that they might love God and fear Him and be rid of any traces of pagan worship, such as the images in their houses, or any evil customs they had learned from the surrounding nations. So he sent five of his princes to teach the people, and these had civil authority, that is, so that the people would understand that these teachings were approved by the king, and the people would respect God and the command of their king.

entries.section: (2) His teaching of the Law to the people

paragraphs.text: Jehoshaphat also sent two priests and with them nine Levites, whom he chose, perhaps because of their distinction in the Law and their excellence in the ability to teach, and they went about the cities of the kingdom of Judah teaching the people the Law of God, having with them a copy of the Law of God, of which one copy was kept with the king and another in the house of the Lord.
From this Jehoshaphat's wisdom appears, who was convinced that any revival in his kingdom must be built on the people's knowledge of the Law of God and walking by it.

Take care to teach your children and loved ones the word of God, in the proper way, for this is your responsibility, and God will hold you accountable for it, and this is more fitting for you than complaining about the wrong behavior of your children and loved ones; and take care to be the first to carry out the word of God, before you teach it to others.

entries.section: (3) His strength and the nations' submission to him

paragraphs.text: When God saw Jehoshaphat's faithfulness in his worship of God and his keeping His commandments, He blessed him and gave him awe in the eyes of all the kingdoms of the nations around him, so they honored him and feared him and did not try to fight him. Thus God fulfilled His promise that He spoke in the Law of Moses (Deut 11:22-25).

entries.section: (3) His strength and the nations' submission to him

paragraphs.text: Burden: what an animal, such as a donkey or a mule, can carry on its back.

The nations did not only honor Jehoshaphat and hold him in awe, but also tried to appease him by bringing him gifts, so some of the Philistines brought a burden of silver and various gifts, and the Arabs brought seven thousand seven hundred rams and the same number of he-goats. The number seven signifies perfection, like the seven sacraments; that is, the nations offered complete love and submission to Jehoshaphat.

entries.section: (3) His strength and the nations' submission to him

paragraphs.text: Jehoshaphat's activity appears in his building of castles beside the cities, and he also built store cities, to suffice for the needs of the kingdom of Judah. And this shows two things:
1- God's blessing and support for Jehoshaphat.
2- Jehoshaphat's greatness among the nations and his strength.

entries.section: (3) His strength and the nations' submission to him

paragraphs.text: And Jehoshaphat's activity was not limited to what preceded in (v. 12), but he did many works in Jerusalem, which are not mentioned here in detail. And he prepared a strong army of mighty warriors to guard Jerusalem. The number of warriors in it was one million one hundred and sixty thousand, under the command of five skilled commanders. And one of them, Amasiah, is mentioned as having offered himself willingly to the Lord, that is, his heart was occupied with the Lord and he performed His service before serving the king. In addition to this, there was another number of soldiers whom Jehoshaphat placed in the various cities of Judah to guard them.

How beautiful it is to be active, doing your work with zeal and not being lazy, for you will receive blessings from God and feel happiness and succeed, and God will even give you awe and favor in the eyes of those around you.
We can summarize the characteristics of Jehoshaphat mentioned in this chapter as follows:

1- Wise: in fortifying his kingdom, especially the northern cities facing the kingdom of Israel, so that the deviant religious thought of idol worship would not seep from Israel into his kingdom of Judah (vv. 1, 2).
2- Keeping the commandments of the Lord and His worship: he refused the worship of idols and worshiped the Lord, like David, and kept the commandments of God (vv. 3, 4).
3- Honored: God gave him stability in his kingdom and the submission of his people to him (v. 5).
4- A teacher of the Law: he sent the princes, the priests and the Levites to teach the people the Law, so that they would be firm in the worship of God (vv. 7-9).
5- Great among the nations: the nations feared him and did not fight him, but brought him gifts to appease him (vv. 10, 11).
6- Active: he built castles and store cities and had many works to magnify Jerusalem, the capital of his kingdom (vv. 12, 13).
7- Strong: he had a great army in Jerusalem and in all the cities of Judah.
Note: see the life of Jehoshaphat at the end of this book.
Jehoshaphat's alliance with Ahab to recover Ramoth-gilead

entries.section: (1) The agreement of Jehoshaphat and Ahab

paragraphs.text: God's blessing on Jehoshaphat continued, so he became very rich, but he thought of relying on the powers of the world, so he made a marriage alliance with Ahab king of Israel, that is, he married his son Jehoram to Athaliah the daughter of Ahab. This was a great mistake, for it was a betrayal of God, who had magnified him greatly, and consequently there was no need to ally himself with a wicked king who worshiped idols, because Ahab was the most wicked of the kings of Israel. This mistake exposed Jehoshaphat to death, but God rescued him for the sake of his goodness, mentioned in the previous chapter, yet it corrupted his kingdom, because the daughter of Ahab brought the worship of idols into the kingdom of Judah; she was a wicked woman and reigned over Judah, and then was killed. Thus we see that Jehoshaphat's wealth made him attached to money and greatness, so he neglected the Law of God and allied himself with idol worshipers. Perhaps Jehoshaphat thought that by his marriage alliance with Ahab he would reach a union of the two kingdoms, but his mistake was that he did not consult God in this matter, so he did not reach union, but corrupted the kingdom of Judah as well.

Always thank God for the gifts He has given you, because all the capabilities you have are a gift of God, which He can withdraw from you if you neglect His commandments. As you have abandoned Him, He can abandon you, perhaps that you may repent and not lose your eternity. So why expose yourself to afflictions? Be precise, holding fast to the commandments of God in His Church all your life.

entries.section: (1) The agreement of Jehoshaphat and Ahab

paragraphs.text: Jerusalem was built on hills; therefore it says that Jehoshaphat went down and traveled to Samaria, the capital of the kingdom of Israel, and this was some years after he began to reign, during which he had reached great eminence. Ahab considered this visit very great, so he killed many sacrifices for Jehoshaphat and made a great feast for him and all who were with him. And Ahab took advantage of this opportunity and asked Jehoshaphat to ally with him in fighting the Arameans to recover the city of Ramoth-gilead, which lies east of the Jordan River in the tribe of Gad, and which the Arameans had taken. Perhaps Ahab seduced Jehoshaphat by saying that this alliance between the two kingdoms would benefit them against the surrounding nations, so Jehoshaphat agreed.

entries.section: (1) Jehu the seer's rebuke of Jehoshaphat

paragraphs.text: After Jehoshaphat escaped from his war with the Arameans, in which Ahab died, he fell into another mistake, which was his alliance with Joram king of Israel, the grandson of Ahab, in his war against Moab (2 Kgs 3:7), which is not mentioned in the Book of Chronicles; then after this he returned to Jerusalem in peace, that is, no bodily harm came to him, but he lost his inner peace as a result of his association with the wicked and God's abandoning him.

At first sight we understand from this verse that Jehoshaphat, after returning from his war in which he allied with Ahab against the Arameans, returned to Jerusalem; but the truth, as we have explained, is that Jehoshaphat's return to Jerusalem in this verse was after his war in which he allied with Joram against Moab, and we understood this from the following verses, which show God's rebuke of him and his repentance, until the end of his life and his keeping away from alliance with the kingdom of Israel.

entries.section: (1) Jehu the seer's rebuke of Jehoshaphat

paragraphs.text: Jehu the son of Hanani the seer: a prophet, the son of Hanani the seer, who rebuked Asa, and he imprisoned him (ch. 16:10). And Jehu is the one who rebuked Baasha king of Israel (1 Kgs 16:1-4). When Jehoshaphat returned to Jerusalem after his alliance with Ahab, and then with Joram his grandson, Jehu the son of Hanani the seer went out to him with a rebuke from God, and said to him: How do you help Ahab and Joram his grandson, the wicked, and how dare you love those who hate the Lord, who worshiped idols and rejected God? Therefore, God is angry with you. And this actually happened, because despite Jehoshaphat's repentance, his return to God and his reforms, God's wrath was upon the offspring of Jehoshaphat, that is, his son Jehoram, who walked in evil, for he killed his brothers and the princes of his people; then Athaliah the wife of Jehoram, the son of Jehoshaphat, came and helped her son Ahaziah in evil and reigned after his death, and killed all the royal offspring except Joash, who escaped. And because God accepted Jehoshaphat's repentance and goodness, He did not punish him in his lifetime.
We see here God's care for Jehoshaphat: he is a good king, but he slipped into alliance with the wicked, so God did not leave him, but sent him a prophet to rebuke him, so that he would repent.

God loves you, even after you sin, and calls you to repentance and rebukes you, or allows afflictions for you so that you return to Him. So may you take heed and return quickly, to regain God's compassion and His care for you.

entries.section: (1) Jehu the seer's rebuke of Jehoshaphat

paragraphs.text: Jehu continued his words to Jehoshaphat and drew him on, saying that God has not forgotten your love for Him and your removal of the worship of idols, that is, the altars and the groves, and your care for the worship of God. We see here God's encouragement of His children, even as He rebukes them, to give them hope of repentance. For despite rebuking Jehoshaphat for his alliance with the wicked, He says to him that there is a good thing in you, which is your love for God and your refusal of the worship of idols.

Jehoshaphat submitted to the word of God through Jehu, and repented of his sins, so he stayed in Jerusalem and began to care for the spiritual life of his people. He took care of the people in Jerusalem, then visited all the kingdom of Judah from its south at Beersheba to its north in the mountain of Ephraim, and so we see Jehoshaphat's concern to visit all the cities of his kingdom himself, to bring the people back to God and call them to repentance. Perhaps his preoccupation with the alliance with the kings of Israel made him neglect the care of his people, in addition to the fact that Athaliah the daughter of Ahab, who married Jehoram the son of Jehoshaphat, was very wicked, and perhaps she spread the worship of idols in Jerusalem and its surroundings. And Jehoshaphat's concern to call his people to repentance is clear evidence of his repentance, and an attempt to repair the effects of his mistakes. As the people were made to stumble because Jehoshaphat mixed with idol worship, so he takes care to call them to repentance.

Jehoshaphat had sent princes, priests and Levites to teach the people (ch. 17:7-9), but the people's straying from the Law made Jehoshaphat appoint judges in all the cities of Judah, to judge by the Law of God in all disputes, and to pass sentence on the wrongdoers who refused to return to the Lord; for the number of judges previously existing was small, so out of Jehoshaphat's concern he appointed many judges in every place.
Jehoshaphat gave the judges a set of instructions when he sent them to judge the children of Israel, which are:

1- That their work in judging is for God and not for man, and this makes their work of the utmost importance and seriousness, because it is offered to God before it is offered to man, so they must do it with uprightness of heart and all exactness (v. 6).
2- He promised them that God would support them and guide them in every problem and encourage and strengthen them (v. 6).
3- He promised them that God would give them awe in the eyes of the people, so they would respect them and submit to them (v. 7).
4- He warned them not to wrong anyone, or show partiality to anyone, or take a bribe (bribery), for they must be representatives of God, who rejects injustice, partiality and bribery (v. 7).

5- After Jehoshaphat visited the cities of Judah and appointed judges in them (v. 5), he established a high court in Jerusalem of the priests, the Levites and the heads of the fathers, to settle the great disputes, and commanded the judges to refer to the supreme kingdom in everything that was too hard for them to decide in the cities of Judah (v. 8).
6- He commanded them to do their work with the fear of God in their hearts, so that they would act with all faithfulness (v. 9).

7- The judges must warn the people against transgressing the Law of God, so that they do not trespass against Him, and God's wrath come upon them, especially since Jehoshaphat had experienced the seriousness of sin, which brought God's wrath upon him (v. 2); so he warns his people, that they may not fall as he fell (v. 10).

8- He appointed two to administer these courts, whether in Jerusalem or in the cities of Judah, namely Amariah the priest and Zebadiah the civil ruler, and the priest and the civil ruler are helped by the officers, that is, the Levites who know the Law. Thus he supported the courts with civil authority, alongside the religious authority represented by the priests and the Levites, so that there would be complete discipline in his kingdom.

Among the evidences of Jehoshaphat's repentance and return to the Lord is that he repeated the word "the Lord" nine times in these verses (vv. 4-11). We see in these instructions Jehoshaphat's wisdom, his exactness and his organization of the courts, in assigning each person his responsibility, whether civil officials, or priests and Levites, whether in Jerusalem or in all the cities of Judah, and his sound administration and God's support of him appear.

Let the word of God be your measure in your conduct. Read the Holy Bible every day and choose a verse to be a message to you from God, to apply in your life. And review yourself at the end of each day by the word of God that you read, and offer repentance for everything in which you sinned, and you will obtain God's mercies and be made worthy to receive the sacraments of confession and Holy Communion.
Jehoshaphat's victory over Moab and the children of Ammon

entries.section: (1) Moab and the children of Ammon try to fight Jehoshaphat

paragraphs.text: Moab: they are the offspring of Lot by his elder daughter, and they lived east of the Dead Sea and were at enmity with the people of God for most of their days.
The children of Ammon: they are the offspring of Lot by his younger daughter, and they lived north of Moab, east of the Jordan River, and were at enmity with the people of God for most of their days.

The Ammonites (Meunim): most likely what is meant is the Ammonites, as in the Jerusalem Bible (the Jesuit translation), and they are some tribes of the Edomites, who lived in Mount Seir; they are the offspring of Esau (Edom), and lived south of the kingdom of Judah. After Jehoshaphat's reforms and his return to God with all his heart and his reforms, Satan stirred up the surrounding nations against him, and God allowed this so that He might be glorified in him, so the Moabites and the children of Ammon, who lived east of the land of the Jews, and likewise the Edomites, who lived south of their land, rose against him; that is, they all united to fight the kingdom of Judah. The reasons for the enemies' attack are not mentioned, and perhaps the reason was their greed for the wealth of the kingdom of Judah.

entries.section: (1) Moab and the children of Ammon try to fight Jehoshaphat

paragraphs.text: Hazazon-tamar: the ancient name of En-gedi, which lies in the kingdom of Judah, west of the Dead Sea and near it.

Jehoshaphat's guards were informed of military movements by the Moabites, the children of Ammon and Edom, and that they had gathered at En-gedi, that is, the south of the kingdom of Judah, and this means that the armies of Moab and the children of Ammon moved to the south of the kingdom of Judah, to unite with the armies of the Edomites and gather for war there.
And the word Aram, mentioned here, means Edom, as in the Jesuit translation.

Do not be disturbed by the plots of the wicked, for God does not allow them to wrong you except to the extent that you can bear, and He gives you the ability to triumph over them, so that He is glorified in you and you stand firm in your faith.

When Jehoshaphat learned of his enemies' preparation to fight him, he was not disturbed but turned to God, as Jehu the son of Hanani had taught him, so he did not try to take refuge in men by allying with them (ch. 19:2); he feared God, therefore he did not fear men, for he felt that the power of God is above every power, and he turned to Him in prayer.
Jehoshaphat joined his prayer with fasting, so he proclaimed a fast for all the kingdom of Judah and offered a prayer for his people before God, because the king here represents the whole people.

The word of God is clear: that the race of Satan has no strength against prayer and fasting. Therefore in all your afflictions, take refuge in prayer and fasting, to declare your destitution before God and your need of Him alone; then you will find help beyond all imagination, supporting you from God.

When the people of the kingdom of Judah learned of the collective fast and prayer, they came to Jerusalem, to the temple of God, to offer prayer and fasting before Him, confident of His promises, which He declared, that against any attack of the enemies, if they lift up their hearts in prayer before Him, He will surely intervene and rescue them (Deut 20:4, 1 Kgs 8:44, 45).

The people of the kingdom of Judah gathered in a new court built at the temple, which perhaps Asa, Jehoshaphat's father, prepared or renewed (ch. 15:8), and it may be the great court, that is, the large one, in the temple, and Jehoshaphat stood before them to pray on their behalf before God, that He might rescue them from their enemies.
Jehoshaphat began his prayer by glorifying God, who has authority over heaven and earth, and all kingdoms are subject to Him, for He has complete power and no one can resist Him.
Friend: a companion.

Jehoshaphat reminds God that He drove out the pagan nations from the land of Canaan and gave their land to His people, the offspring of His friend Abraham; so he reminds God of His care and love for His people, and reminds Him also of His beloved Abraham, interceding by him, that God might have mercy on them and rescue them from their enemies.
And he says that God's covenants are firm forever, "I gave them ... forever"; therefore he pleads with Him to intervene, to repel the enemies from them.

He reminds God that His people built a temple for Him in the land of Canaan, and that He promised Solomon, when he built this temple, that if the sword of judgment came upon them, that is, an attack by enemies, or any affliction, such as famine and pestilence, He would quickly intervene and rescue His people.
The land of Seir: that is, of the Edomites.

Jehoshaphat declared to God the seriousness of the attack of a great army from the alliance of Moab, the children of Ammon and Edom, whom God had commanded His people, when entering to possess the land of Canaan, not to attack, but to go around their lands, because they were their cousins (Deut 2:5-7). But sadly these enemies did not keep the kindness of the people of God to them and attacked them to drive them out of their possession; therefore Jehoshaphat asks God to rescue them from these wicked aggressors. And this land, the land of Canaan, God had given to His people, so the attempt of the Moabites and those with them to drive the people of God out of it is a challenge to God and resistance to Him, the giver of the land, and consequently God's intervention is required to rescue His people and establish them in their land.
Jehoshaphat specified his petition to God, which was to intervene to rescue His people from their enemies, and he declared to God the following:

A- The weakness of his people before the strength of the enemies, that is, his people's great need of God, and it is clear from this that Jehoshaphat did not rely on his many soldiers, who exceeded a million (ch. 17:14-18), but relied on God alone, and we did not hear that Jehoshaphat took care to prepare his armies, but he took care to pray, to obtain God's help.
