Be assured that your good works and your conduct as a child of God affect those around you more than any words. So worship God with all your heart and offer your love to those around you, for your life is the Gospel lived out, which proclaims Christ to those around you.

The number of the sacrifices offered as burnt offerings, that is, burned entirely to God, was large: seventy bulls, a hundred rams and two hundred lambs. This shows that a great number of the people had their hearts filled with the love of God, as we mentioned in (v. 31).

And the rest of the sacrifices, besides the burnt offerings, were six hundred oxen and three thousand sheep, and this is a large number which shows the people's turning to repentance and the worship of God.

The number of the priests was small, perhaps because of King Hezekiah's quick beginning in cleansing the house of the Lord and sanctifying it, for some of the priests hastened to come to Jerusalem and purify themselves in preparation for service, while the rest delayed. But the Levites were quicker in responding to the call of King Hezekiah, for they were more upright and more concerned with renewing the service in the house of the Lord. Therefore, because of the abundance of the sacrifices and the fewness of the priests, the priests needed the Levites' help in flaying the sacrifices, so that they might offer them on the bronze altar before God.

Although King Hezekiah's command was sudden for the priests and Levites and all the people, that they should hasten to cleanse and sanctify the temple and restore the worship in it, the Spirit of the Holy God moved the hearts of many of the people, so they came and offered sacrifices and rejoiced at the return of worship in the holy temple.
The restoration of the feasts of the Passover and Unleavened Bread: King Hezekiah, at the beginning of his reign, took care of matters that show his goodness, which are:
1- In the first month he took care to cleanse and sanctify the temple and to offer sacrifices, and these signify repentance and the examination of the soul.

2- In the second month he called for the keeping of the Passover, which is one of the important feasts, which signify Christ the Redeemer, and all the people keep it, and it signifies partaking of the Body and Blood of the Lord.

entries.section: (1) The call to Judah and the tribes to keep the Passover

paragraphs.text: King Hezekiah's fatherhood appears in his care for all the people of God, whether in his own kingdom, which is the southern kingdom of Judah, or in the northern kingdom, most of whose people had been taken captive by Assyria. So he sent letters calling everyone to come to Jerusalem to keep the Passover, as the Law prescribes. He did not send to Judah only, but to Manasseh and Ephraim, because Ephraim represents a large tribe, and so signifies the whole northern kingdom of Israel.

entries.section: (1) The call to Judah and the tribes to keep the Passover

paragraphs.text: King Hezekiah wanted to restore the celebration of the feast of the Passover, but he was not able to keep it at its appointed time in the first month, because he was occupied with cleansing the temple and sanctifying the altar, and because not all the Levites and priests had sanctified themselves. So Hezekiah gathered his counselors to decide when to keep the Passover, and they had three choices before them:

1- To keep the Passover at its appointed time, which is the fourteenth day of the first month, but the priests and Levites who had come to Jerusalem and were prepared for the Passover were few in number, in addition to the difficulty of gathering all the people to Jerusalem at that time.
2- To postpone the celebration of the feast of the Passover to the coming year, but the postponement would be long, and the people might lose their spiritual zeal.

3- The Law provides that whoever is unclean, or on a long journey, at the time of the feast of the Passover in the first month, may keep the Passover on the fourteenth day of the second month (Num 9:10, 11). Hezekiah and his counselors settled on the third choice, since they had about a month before them, during which Hezekiah sent messengers to all the priests and Levites to sanctify themselves, and to gather the people in the kingdom of Judah and the rest of the tribes.

entries.section: (1) The call to Judah and the tribes to keep the Passover

paragraphs.text: Beersheba: A city lying in the far south of the kingdom of Judah.
Dan: A tribe that dwelt in a region in the far north toward the Sea of Galilee.

Hezekiah sent messengers from himself to all the land where the children of Israel dwelt, from the far south, where the city of Beersheba is, to the far north, where the tribe of Dan dwells, to call all the people to come to Jerusalem to keep the Passover, as it is written in the Law of Moses (Ex 12:1-14), especially since the people of God had neglected the celebration of the feast of the Passover for a long time, from the days of Solomon, for it is not mentioned in the Holy Bible that such a Passover was kept since the days of Solomon (v. 26).

entries.section: (1) The call to Judah and the tribes to keep the Passover

paragraphs.text: The couriers who had in their hands letters from King Hezekiah and his princes who assisted him went out and ran to all the cities of Judah and Israel, calling them in the name of the Lord God of their fathers, Abraham, Isaac and Israel, that is, Jacob, to return to Him and worship Him faithfully and keep the feast of the Passover, because God had delivered them from the hand of Assyria and they had remained in their cities, while their brethren had been taken captive by Assyria to scattered lands in the Assyrian kingdom; for the Assyrian captivity took place in stages at the hands of more than one king, so he says, "out of the hand of the kings of Assyria."
Here spiritual matters appear, which are:
1- Hezekiah's care for all the people of Israel and not only those in the kingdom of Judah, as we mentioned.
2- He calls his people to return to God to keep the feast of the Passover, that is, to return to their faith and their worship of God, and so obtain His blessing and care.
3- He reminds them of God's grace toward them, that He delivered them, without their brethren, from the Assyrian captivity, so they must thank Him and worship Him faithfully.

entries.section: (1) The call to Judah and the tribes to keep the Passover

paragraphs.text: Astonishment: People came to be astonished and to marvel when they passed through the land of Israel, which Assyria had destroyed, taking many of its people captive.
Be ye not stiffnecked: The stubborn animal stiffens its neck, that is, it refuses to submit to its owner and to do the works required of it.
The king added these matters in his letters:
1- A call to the people to repent and remember the sins of their fathers, which led to this captivity.

2- A warning against continuing to refuse the worship of God, that is, being unfaithful to Him and occupied with the worship of idols and the lusts of the world, lest they be exposed to destruction a second time, as Assyria did to them.
3- Putting an end to their rebellion against God and their refusal of His worship, since for a long time they had not kept the feast of the Passover.
4- Calling them to come to Jerusalem, to enter the temple of God and worship Him and celebrate the Passover.
5- He gives them the good news that their return to God and His worship removes God's wrath from them and they will be freed from the Assyrian captivity.

6- He warns them that their return to God and their worship of Him brings a blessing to their captive brethren, who had begun to repent and long to return to the temple of God and could not; and when God sees their return, He has compassion on their brethren and brings them back from captivity. For among the clear attributes of God is His great compassion toward the repentant, as He softens the hearts of those who held them captive, so they bring them back to their land, and this is what happened by the hand of Cyrus the Persian king.

Repentance is the way of deliverance, which rescues you from all your sins and the troubles that result from them, so hasten to it and do not be lax. On the other hand, do not despair, however grave your sins, because God loves you and waits for you.

The couriers set out to all the land of Israel, which is expressed here by Manasseh and Ephraim, but they reached the land possessed by the tribe of Zebulun and did not continue their way northward to Dan and Naphtali. Perhaps this was because of the large presence of the people of God in the region as far as Zebulun, or some obstacles that prevented the couriers from reaching the far north.

Strangely, the children of Israel strongly rejected the king's letters, and even laughed to scorn and mocked his messengers, that is, the couriers, because their hearts were attached to the pagan gods and their places of worship, and they forgot their true God, whom their fathers had worshipped.

But a small number of them were moved by the king's letters and promised to come to Jerusalem to keep the Passover, for they felt their sins in forsaking the worship of God, and humbled themselves before Him and wanted to return to His worship.

Although the Jews in the northern kingdom refused to respond to the king's letters, a small number of them responded, humbled themselves and wanted to return to God. Therefore, servant of God, let there be hope in you that your service is accepted by God and that a small number may respond to it, despite the refusal of the majority. So offer your love and your service and do not be hindered because people reject your words, for God in the end will bring those who are ready, and they are the ones He has chosen.

In the kingdom of Judah the people responded to the king's letters and had one heart in returning to God and worshipping Him, so they traveled to Jerusalem. A great multitude gathered and the city was filled with lovers of God and His worship, to keep the feast of the Passover and the feast of Unleavened Bread which follows it, in the second month. Thus the work of God appears, who moved the hearts in the kingdom of Judah to encourage Hezekiah and gladden his heart.

The first thing done by the multitude of God's people gathered in Jerusalem was that they removed the pagan altars which the former wicked kings had set up in Jerusalem. For there must be repentance and purity before enjoying the worship of God and fellowship with Him. And they cast the remains of these altars, on which they had offered sacrifices and incense to the idols, into the brook Kidron, which lies east and south of Jerusalem.

They stood in their place: The priests and Levites performed their service, each one in his own service. When the priests and Levites saw the zeal and fervor of the people in removing the worship of idols, they were ashamed of their laziness, because they ought to have been leading the people in getting rid of the remains of pagan worship. And the priests and Levites sanctified themselves and began to kill the sacrifices and sprinkle their blood in the temple, as the Levites brought the blood of the sacrifices to the priests, and they sprinkled it on the bronze altar.

Thus the priests and Levites returned to performing their service, as prescribed by the Law of Moses, with all care and commitment, and they completed the feast of the Passover on the fourteenth day of the second month.

A small number of the people of Israel, coming from the tribes outside the kingdom of Judah, responded and came to Jerusalem to keep the Passover, but they had not sanctified themselves according to the Law. So the Levites offered their sacrifices for them, and King Hezekiah prayed to God for them, that He would accept their return to Him despite their weakness in not being sanctified; for when they ate the Passover, God struck them with diseases because of their laxity, but through Hezekiah's prayer God healed them and forgave them for two reasons:
1- Their repentance and return to God and their abandoning the worship of idols, so they prepared their hearts for the worship of God.
2- The intercession and prayer of Hezekiah for them.
Those who were prudent: Those who understood God's Law.

After the priests and Levites and the people had killed the Passover and kept the feast of the Passover, they began, according to the Law, to keep the feast of Unleavened Bread for seven days, eating unleavened bread and not leavened bread, because leaven signifies evil and unleavened bread signifies purity of heart. And the number seven signifies perfection of purity.
During the seven days the Levite singers praised God in His holy temple in great joy. For whoever lives in purity, that is, eats the unleavened bread, can launch out into the praise of God.

And King Hezekiah came forward to encourage the priests and Levites, who understood God's Law and who had grieved greatly in the days of the former wicked kings because of the neglect of the worship of God; and through Hezekiah's words they regained their confidence and their faith and were encouraged and rejoiced greatly at the return of the celebration of God's feasts. Perhaps the Levites also rejoiced at the return of a number of their brethren from the tribes to the worship of God in Jerusalem.

Because of the great joy of God's people at returning to Him and holding the celebration of the feasts of the Passover and Unleavened Bread, the congregation took counsel and agreed to extend the celebration another week, in addition to what the Law prescribes, especially since the king gave the people a thousand bulls and seven thousand sheep. And the princes also gave a thousand bulls and ten thousand sheep, so it was a very great religious celebration, and a large number of priests were sanctified, so they were able to offer many sacrifices to God.

Although the middle of the second month is the time of harvest, the people's occupation and joy in the worship of God made them extend the celebration another week, that is, they cared for their spiritual life before their material life. And we see the abundance of the gifts of the king and the princes; although the kingdom was poor, they all gave generously and out of their need, and therefore God must have blessed them because of their great love.
The strangers: The Gentiles who dwelt with the tribes of Israel and became Jews.

The people of God rejoiced, whether those dwelling in the kingdom of Judah, or those coming from the tribes of Israel, and also the stranger proselytes who dwelt among them, because they kept the great feast of the Passover and the feast of Unleavened Bread, especially since no celebration of these feasts with such magnificence had been held since the days of King Solomon, for they kept the feast two weeks, like the days of the dedication of the temple in the time of Solomon, and offered sacrifices in abundance.

And the prayers of the people went up, led by the Levites, before the temple of God, so God rejoiced in them, and the priests the Levites blessed the people on behalf of God, and joy and gladness filled the hearts of all.

Joy is your natural state as a child of God. If you are occupied with the love of God and His worship, then you can cast all your cares upon Him and feel His hand supporting you and bringing you through the afflictions while you keep your peace and your joy.
The people's offerings and their distribution

entries.section: (2) The offering of the tithes and their gathering

paragraphs.text: The gates of the tents of the Lord: The gates of the temple.

Hezekiah took care to organize the service in the temple according to what David and Solomon had arranged, and distributed the responsibilities among the priests and Levites, whether in offering the sacrifices, or in the praise, or in any other service.

entries.section: (2) The offering of the tithes and their gathering

paragraphs.text: Since worship in the temple had been neglected, the temple was empty of gifts, whether sacrifices or offerings; therefore Hezekiah gave from his own money to complete the worship, which was the morning and evening burnt offerings, and also those offered on the sabbaths and at the new moons and the appointed feasts. And by this he became an example to his people in giving gifts to the house of the Lord.

By this Hezekiah's goodness appears, for he was not content with cleansing the temple, nor with beginning the worship in it and sanctifying the altar, but held the feasts of the Passover and Unleavened Bread and encouraged the people to worship God, and also took care for the continuation of the daily worship of God in the temple and the provision of its material needs.

entries.section: (2) The offering of the tithes and their gathering

paragraphs.text: Hezekiah's second concern for providing gifts for the house of the Lord appeared in his asking the people dwelling in Jerusalem to give the tithes to God, to provide for the needs of the priests and Levites, that they might be free for the service of God and hold fast to God's Law, which prescribes being devoted to His service; for in the period of neglect of the worship of God in the days of the wicked kings, the priests and Levites were occupied with the works of the world to provide for their necessary needs.

entries.section: (2) The offering of the tithes and their gathering

paragraphs.text: New wine (must): Wine.

Heaps: Piles. The command of King Hezekiah reached not only the regions of the kingdom of Judah, but also the tribes, so the children of Israel, dwelling outside the kingdom of Judah and inside it, took care to give the tithes of wheat, wine, oil, honey and all the produce of the field, and also of the animals, such as oxen and sheep; and because of the abundance of the gifts, they gathered them in heaps.
We notice the abundance of the gifts, and this is a proof of two things:
1- The people's care and religious zeal, so they carried out the commandment and gave the tithes and more than that.
2- When God saw the love of His people, He blessed their harvests, their crops and their cattle, so they became abundant.

entries.section: (2) The offering of the tithes and their gathering

paragraphs.text: The priests and Levites began to arrange the heaps of gifts, putting each kind of gift by itself, and the gifts continued to increase from the third month, when the wheat is harvested, to the seventh month, in which they gathered the fruits of the various trees. Then King Hezekiah himself came, with the princes of his kingdom, and they saw the abundance of the heaps, so they rejoiced greatly and thanked God, and blessed the people and thanked them for their love and care in carrying out God's commandment.

entries.section: (2) The offering of the tithes and their gathering

paragraphs.text: The priests came before Hezekiah, with their chief Azariah, who was of the descendants of Zadok the priest, who lived in the days of David, and Azariah told him of the abundance of the gifts and that the priests and Levites had eaten and been satisfied from them and that this abundance, arranged in heaps, overflowed, and that this was due to God's blessing upon the people and their love and obedience to His commandment.

The blessing of the Lord is great for everyone who loves Him, so that he has need of nothing; therefore be careful to give the tithes and the firstfruits, that you may rejoice in God's care and blessings, and above all that your heart may be filled with His love and you may live in fellowship with God that cannot be expressed.

entries.section: (3) The storehouses and the portions of the priests and Levites

paragraphs.text: Chambers: Storehouses.

Hezekiah commanded that chambers be prepared inside the house of the Lord, to be storehouses in which the tithes and all the offerings that the people had given would be put. And he appointed two of the Levites, Cononiah and Shimei his brother, to organize the storehouses, and Hezekiah, with the help of the high priest, also appointed ten Levites to help them in this work.

We notice that the gathering of the gifts and their storing was done faithfully by all those in charge, and this of course gladdens the heart of God, so He blesses them, and at the head of all these was the good King Hezekiah.

entries.section: (3) The storehouses and the portions of the priests and Levites

paragraphs.text: The most holy things: The part of the offerings and sacrifices which is given to the priests and which they eat in the temple (Lev 2:3, 10, 7:6). Likewise Hezekiah and Azariah the high priest appointed a chief over the porters, Kore the son of Imnah the Levite, and set him over the east gate, which is the main gate leading to the temple. His responsibility was to distribute the portions of the priests in the temple and Jerusalem from the offerings and sacrifices, which they must eat in the holy place, that is, beside the temple.

Hezekiah also appointed six Levites to help Kore, to distribute portions to the priests and Levites who dwelt in the cities of the kingdom of Judah; for the priests were divided into twenty-four courses, each of which performed the service of the temple for two weeks each year, and the rest of the year they dwelt in their cities, far from Jerusalem. So care began for the needs of the priests and Levites, that they might remain free for the service of God and not need to do the works of the world for their food. And they distributed the portions to all, great and small, that is, the distribution was done faithfully and with care for every individual.

entries.section: (3) The storehouses and the portions of the priests and Levites

paragraphs.text: Those whom King Hezekiah appointed took care to distribute the portions to the priests and Levites, to all the priests and Levites who were recorded in their genealogies, and also their children and their wives, and they cared for the great and the small to satisfy all, whether those who serve in Jerusalem or those who dwell in the cities of the priests and Levites, whom the lot had not appointed to the service of the house of the Lord.

Thus we see that, because of the faithfulness of the priests and Levites, who sanctified themselves and cared for the service of the house of the Lord, God blessed them and gave them all their needs, by putting this care in the heart of the good King Hezekiah.

entries.section: (3) The storehouses and the portions of the priests and Levites

paragraphs.text: From all that has gone before, the goodness of King Hezekiah appears in the following:
1- His care for the service in the house of the Lord.
2- His holding fast to the commandments and the Law.
3- His faithfulness and exactness in carrying out God's commands.

Your goodness and God's acceptance of you are based on the extent of your obedience to His commandments and your faithfulness in carrying them out, so do not be troubled by your weaknesses as long as you try and strive and press on in God's way, for He knows your heart and blesses you in all your steps.
The crushing of the Assyrians and the healing of Hezekiah

After all the faithfulness of Hezekiah and his people to God in cleansing their land of idolatrous worship, sanctifying the Temple and restoring the religious celebrations, the feasts of the Passover and Unleavened Bread, Hezekiah was surprised by the attack of Sennacherib king of Assyria, who was dominating the world at that time. He attacked the cities of the kingdom of Judah and coveted the fall of Jerusalem and the taking of the whole kingdom of Judah, just as he and the kings before him had seized the northern kingdom of Israel and its capital Samaria only a few days before the days of Hezekiah.
We may wonder that God allowed this great affliction to come upon Hezekiah despite his goodness, but if we are patient, we will understand the following:

1- God postponed this affliction until Hezekiah and his people grew strong, were sanctified and worshipped God faithfully; that is, He did not hinder their positive works and their striving toward God.
2- He allowed this attack to test the faith of Hezekiah and his people, and indeed they prayed and sought God with all their hearts.
3- After this God was greatly glorified in crushing the enemies in a way that the people of God had not imagined, so their faith was established.
Stopped: blocked up and filled in.

When King Hezekiah saw Sennacherib's intention to attack Jerusalem, he took counsel with his leaders, that is, his advisers who lead the people. This shows Hezekiah's concern and his esteem for the opinions of those around him; he was not a despot. After the consultation they agreed on preparations to face Sennacherib; the first was to stop the springs of water around Jerusalem, so that the enemies would find no water to drink and would withdraw from besieging Jerusalem because of their thirst. As for Jerusalem, it had springs of water inside it that supplied it, so it would not suffer thirst if it were besieged, especially since Hezekiah stopped the main spring that supplied Jerusalem and diverted its course from underground into the city (v. 30).

A great number of the men of Judah were enthusiastic and hurried to fill in the springs of water surrounding Jerusalem. There was also a small stream beside Jerusalem, which probably filled with rainwater and no longer exists today, and they filled it in as well, so that when the armies of Assyria came to besiege Jerusalem they would find no water and would be forced to withdraw because of their thirst. Here we see the people's concern to defend their country and their reliance on God, so they advanced courageously, not afraid of the forces of Assyria coming against them.
The stopping of the waters signifies not handing over our abilities to Satan, so that he may use them to destroy us.
To complete the military preparations, Hezekiah rebuilt the broken parts of the wall of Jerusalem and raised it until it reached the towers built on the wall.

He also built another wall around Jerusalem to fortify it and to hinder the enemies from reaching it. He also fortified the citadel, which is a part of Jerusalem called the City of David, or the City of Zion, or the Ophel; it is a strong fortress that is difficult to storm, and from it the enemies can be attacked if they try to storm Jerusalem. Hezekiah also prepared many defensive weapons, such as shields, and offensive weapons as well. This shows the faithfulness of Hezekiah and his people, for they did everything in their power to defend Jerusalem, the holy city.

These fortifications signify the importance of the spiritual person arming himself with spiritual weapons, which are considered like a wall that protects him from the attacks of the enemy; they are his prayers, his readings, his fasts and all the means of grace.

After these preparations Hezekiah did the most important thing, which was to strengthen the faith of his soldiers and encourage them. He gathered the commanders of his armies in the square of Jerusalem and encouraged them that God who is with them is stronger than any enemy, so that they should not be alarmed by the multitude or the strength of Assyria, because God is stronger than the power of men. In this he speaks like Elisha, who encouraged his servant by saying, "they that be with us are more than they that be with them" (2 Kgs 6:16). So the people believed the words of Hezekiah, their faith was established, and they were strengthened and prepared for war.

Be confident that God who is with you is stronger than all the powers of the world, so do not be troubled by the changes of the world or the evil of those around you, for God is able to deliver you from their plots. Hold fast to Him in much prayer, do your duties faithfully and be at peace, for He protects you from every evil.
Lachish: a fortified city in the kingdom of Judah, located west of Hebron, at a distance of fifteen miles.

Sennacherib king of Assyria captured a great city in Judah called Lachish, and then sent his armies to Jerusalem to besiege it and take it. By the hand of his servants Sennacherib sent letters of threat to the people living in Jerusalem and standing on its walls.

Sennacherib sent a threat in the form of an exclamation to the inhabitants of Jerusalem, because they were fortifying themselves inside Jerusalem, declaring to them the futility of their trust in the words of Hezekiah their king, who told them that their God would protect them from Assyria. Sennacherib accused Hezekiah of deceiving his people and exposing them to death by hunger and thirst in Jerusalem, which the Assyrians were besieging and would capture.

Because of his lack of understanding, Sennacherib told the people that Hezekiah had torn down the altars of his God and had called his people to sacrifice and worship before one altar, which is in the house of the Lord. Of course Sennacherib does not understand the difference between God and the pagan gods, and he thinks that tearing down the altars of the idols is tearing down the altars of God.

Sennacherib spoke with arrogance, declaring that he and his fathers had seized all the countries of the world to which they had gone, and that their gods had been unable to protect them from Assyria; therefore the God of the children of Israel would not be able to protect them from the hand of Assyria. The words of Hezekiah, he said, were merely a deception of his people; that is, Sennacherib was affirming the truth of his overwhelming power over all countries, however strong the power of their gods.
This shows the ignorance of Sennacherib, because all the pagan gods are demons and have no value before the power of God, the only true God, the God of Israel.

Do not be troubled by the logic of weak people around you and their reliance on their own strength, for it is nothing before the power of your God. Fortify yourself in Him, seek His help, walk uprightly before Him, and be sure that He protects you and delivers you.

The servants of Sennacherib dared to speak insolently against God and against Hezekiah, more than their king had spoken. And Sennacherib sent letters of threat in which he reviled God and King Hezekiah, affirming his overwhelming power, which would crush Jerusalem.

The servants of Sennacherib cried out with loud voices in the Jews' language, which the people of God understand, to frighten them so that they would submit and surrender like the other countries that had surrendered to Assyria, regarding the God of Israel as merely a god like the rest of the gods of the pagan nations.

The enemies' insulting of Hezekiah in words, as they spoke against God, is a great honor to Hezekiah, that his name was linked with God, and it confirms his goodness. Therefore do not be troubled if the people of the world insult you because you hold fast to God, His commandments and the teachings of the Church.

Hezekiah's prayer and its answer are mentioned in detail in (2 Kgs 19:14-36) and were explained there; here, the writer refers to it briefly, and makes clear how the prayer of King Hezekiah united with Isaiah the prophet and rose up to heaven, so that God might deliver His people from Assyria. This shows who the true friends are, those who appear in time of hardship, for Isaiah was the supporter of Hezekiah in his prayer, and God answered them both and rescued His people, as appears in the following verses.

Be careful in choosing your friends, because spiritual and faithful friends are the ones who remain with you in the midst of affliction, so you are at ease in your friendship with them. How sweet it is to befriend the saints before men, for they help you in your relationship with God and come to your aid in time of hardship.
God answered the prayer of Hezekiah and Isaiah, and sent His angel, who killed the mighty men of the Assyrian army.

The Book of Kings tells us that the number of those killed was one hundred and eighty-five thousand, that is, He destroyed them utterly, so that King Sennacherib fled to his own country and abandoned the siege of Jerusalem. He entered the temple of his god to cry to him for help, and his two sons, who came forth from his own bowels, fell upon him and killed him, and a third son of his, Esarhaddon, took the throne.

Thus God's mockery of the power of the enemies appears, for He destroyed the mighty army that had overrun the whole world but was unable to harm the children of God. Rather, God stretched out His hand and killed the distinguished ones in the army of Sennacherib, killing every mighty man of valor, every leader and every captain, so that the remaining soldiers no longer had any value and were unable to continue besieging Jerusalem.

Sennacherib felt his weakness, since all his helpers had been killed, so he fled lest the angel kill him. But God allowed him to be killed a shameful death while under the protection of his pagan gods and by the hand of his own sons, to be a lesson before all the nations, so that no enemy would try to attack the people of God, because their God is stronger than all the gods.

By destroying the army of Assyria, God saved His people and His holy city Jerusalem, and the fear of the people of God came upon all the nations around it, and consequently they were secure and under the protection of God.

The nations around the kingdom of Judah felt the greatness of King Hezekiah and the power of his God, so they tried to appease Hezekiah by presenting precious gifts and treasures, and he became exceedingly great.

entries.section: (4) The healing of Hezekiah, his constructions, and then his death

paragraphs.text: The events of Hezekiah's sickness, his healing and his pride were mentioned in detail and explained in (2 Kgs 20:1-19), and were also mentioned in (Isa 38, 39). Here he speaks briefly about Hezekiah's illness, until he was close to death, and then he prayed, and God healed him and gave him a sign, which was the shadow going back ten degrees. When a delegation came from Babylon he became proud and showed them his greatness and his treasures, and did not thank God, who had bestowed on him this miraculous healing, but was occupied with his greatness before men. So God's decision, by the mouth of Isaiah, was that all these treasures would be carried to Babylon, and that some of his sons would be taken as slaves to the king of Babylon, but not in the days of Hezekiah; so the king and all the inhabitants of Jerusalem humbled themselves and repented before God. God's punishment took place in this Babylonian captivity, whose direct cause was the departure of the kings and the people from God in the days of the captivity and their refusal to repent, unlike the righteous Hezekiah, who, when he sinned, humbled himself and repented, and his people were influenced by him, so they humbled themselves and repented as he did.

God's love for Hezekiah appears in that He allowed him to be broken and to feel his great weakness before the power of Assyria, and then to be completely broken when death approached him, until he reached death to the world and the emptying of his own will, with no hope except God. So he prayed a deep prayer both times, and here he enjoyed hearing the voice of God, who spoke to him by the mouth of Isaiah; for his experience of hearing God came when he was completely broken. There is no way to enjoy God except by becoming a stranger to the world, rising above its material things and cutting off all desires.

entries.section: (4) The healing of Hezekiah, his constructions, and then his death

paragraphs.text: Stalls: feeding troughs for the cattle in which they eat, that is, stables.

God blessed Hezekiah for his goodness, which was mentioned in (chs. 29-32), and gave him great wealth, so that he made treasuries for silver, gold and precious stones, as well as treasuries for spices and precious vessels, in addition to storehouses for weapons, such as shields. He also made storehouses for grain such as wheat, and storehouses for the wine produced from the many vineyards he owned, and other storehouses for storing oil. God also gave him many cattle, so he made stalls for the oxen, the sheep and all kinds of beasts, and built towers in the midst of these stalls to care for them.
But, sadly, abundance of wealth helped Hezekiah toward pride, so God was angry with him, although at the beginning of his reign, when he was poor, his distinguished goodness appeared.

God's blessings show His love for those who fear Him, and they come in material forms, but when a person matures spiritually He gives him what is greater, that is, spiritual blessings, so he feels God with him and enjoys His fellowship. Be upright and hold fast to God's commandments, and you will enjoy blessings all your days.

entries.section: (4) The healing of Hezekiah, his constructions, and then his death

paragraphs.text: Gihon: a main spring that supplies Jerusalem, located in the Kidron Valley, east of Jerusalem and south of the Temple, and in it, higher than another lower spring in the same place.

Among the most important works Hezekiah did was providing water for the inhabitants of Jerusalem, by making a lower channel underground, that is, a tunnel that comes out of the upper spring of Gihon and enters inside Jerusalem. God blessed this work, which made it difficult to besiege Jerusalem and expose its inhabitants to thirst. God also blessed the works of Hezekiah on account of his piety and goodness.
This lower channel, in which the water flows underground, signifies the hidden work of the Holy Spirit inside the heart, to water it and satisfy it.

entries.section: (4) The healing of Hezekiah, his constructions, and then his death

paragraphs.text: Interpreters: plural of interpreter, meaning a messenger who knows more than one language; here it means the messengers of Babylon, who know the Babylonian and the Jewish languages.

Hezekiah was exposed to two trials: the attack of the army of the Assyrians, and then the trial of his illness and his facing death. In both trials he took refuge in God, who rescued him from the hand of Assyria by sending the angel who killed the mighty men of the Assyrian army. In the mortal illness He healed him and gave him a clear wonder in the whole land, which was the going back of the shadow ten degrees.

But he was exposed to a third trial, which was a test from God, when messengers came to him from Babylon, since they had seen the wonder of the shadow going back, to congratulate him on his healing. Hezekiah fell in the trial and became proud, and showed them his wealth and his treasures and valuables that show his greatness, and did not take refuge in God in prayer before showing them what he had. But he returned and repented, after Isaiah the prophet rebuked him and announced God's punishment for him because of his pride; and when he repented, God made this punishment take place after his lifetime, that is, in the days of his descendants, who departed from God, so the disaster of the Babylonian captivity came upon them.
We notice that the Book of Chronicles here focuses on Hezekiah's goodness and his great works and not his sins, because it presents the righteous kings of Judah as types of Christ.

entries.section: (4) The healing of Hezekiah, his constructions, and then his death

paragraphs.text: His goodness: his good deeds and righteous works.

The details of the life of King Hezekiah and his righteous works are not written in the Holy Bible, but are mentioned in a book called the Vision of Isaiah the prophet, which is among a collection of books called the Book of the Kings of Judah and Israel, and these are historical books and not part of the Holy Bible.

entries.section: (4) The healing of Hezekiah, his constructions, and then his death

paragraphs.text: The chiefest of the sepulchres of the sons of David: the best and greatest place among these tombs.

After that Hezekiah died, and they buried him in the greatest place among the tombs of the City of David. The people of Jerusalem and the kingdom of Judah mourned for him and made many honors for him, perhaps lamentation, dirges and a great burning, as they were accustomed in ancient times, and then his son Manasseh reigned in his place.
Note: See the life of Hezekiah at the end of the book.
Manasseh and Amon, kings of Judah
As a result of Manasseh and his people being immersed in the worship of idols and base lusts, they did not listen to the voice of God, which came by the mouth of the prophets, such as Isaiah.
This shows God's love and concern for sinners, however deeply they are immersed in sin, for He seeks the salvation of all.
Be sure that God loves you and seeks your salvation however far you have gone from Him, but may you respond to His call and return to Him quickly, whatever your sins, for He will forgive you.
Hook: a ring of bronze placed in the nose of slaves or animals, as a sign of their being owned and subject to their master.

God allowed the Assyrians, who ruled the world at that time, to attack the kingdom of Judah and seize King Manasseh, put a hook in his nose like slaves and animals, and bind him with chains, perhaps because of an accusation brought against him of rebelling against the king of Assyria. They took him to Babylon, which was at that time a city under the authority of the king of Assyria.

When Manasseh was greatly distressed and in deep humiliation in the prison of Babylon, being treated like a slave, he came to himself and felt his sins that had caused him all this humiliation, and offered repentance with contrition before God and prayed a deep prayer that the Church reads on the night of Abu Ghalamsis, that is, the Saturday of Joy. It is part of the Holy Bible that was removed from it, but the Church acknowledges it and reads it in its prayers.
And when he repented, God forgave him his sins and restored him to his kingdom in Jerusalem.

The Second Book of Kings did not mention the imprisonment of Manasseh and his prayer, nor his return from Babylon and his reforms, because when he repented he was not able to change the corruption that had spread among the people because of his many evils, and the Book of Kings is concerned with the condition of the people, whereas the Book of Chronicles is concerned with the kings as types of Christ and focuses on the good works they did more than on their evils.

The Prayer of Manasseh (this text is taken from the book of the prayers of Holy Week of the Coptic Orthodox Church) 1 O Lord Almighty, who is in heaven, God of our fathers Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, and of their seed. 2 Who made heaven and earth and all their adornment. 3 Who bound the sea by the word of Your command and sealed its depths with Your fearful name, full of glory, at which everything fears and trembles before the face of Your power. 4 For the greatness of Your glory cannot be measured. 5 And the wrath of Your anger against sinners cannot be withstood. 6 And the mercy of Your will cannot be counted or comprehended; You are the Lord Most High, merciful, long-suffering and abundant in mercy, righteous, and repenting of the evil of men. 7 You also, O Lord, according to Your goodness, have appointed repentance for him who has sinned against You. 8 And in the multitude of Your mercy You have proclaimed repentance to sinners for their salvation. 9 You, O Lord, God of the righteous, did not appoint repentance for the just, Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, who did not sin against You, but You appointed repentance for me, the sinner. 10 For I have sinned more than the number of the sand of the sea. 11 My iniquities are multiplied, and I am not worthy to lift up my eyes to heaven because of the multitude of my unrighteousness. 12 But I bow down because of the multitude of my iron bonds, and I cannot lift up my head because of my sins. 13 And now in truth I have provoked You, and there is no rest for me, for I have angered Your wrath; I have done evil in Your hands, and I have not done Your will, nor kept Your commandments, but I have set up my abominations and multiplied my defilements. 14 And now I bend the knees of my heart and ask of Your goodness: I have sinned, O Lord, I have sinned, and my iniquities I know. But I ask and beseech You, O Lord, forgive me, and do not destroy me with my iniquities, nor be angry with me forever, nor hold my evils against me, nor cast me into judgment in the depth beneath the earth. 15 For You are the God of those who repent. 16 And in me show Your goodness, for I am unworthy. 17 And save me according to the multitude of Your mercy, and I will praise You continually all the days of my life. 18 For You are the One to whom all the powers of the heavens sing. 19 To You is the glory forever, Amen.

The Prayer of Manasseh (this text is taken from the book of the prayers of Holy Week of the Coptic Orthodox Church) This prayer is acknowledged by the Orthodox and Catholic Churches, and it is a prayer known since the Apostolic age and found in the Septuagint translation of the books of the Old Testament, and the Coptic Orthodox Church reads it among the prayers selected from the Holy Bible on the night of the Saturday of Joy after Great Friday. This prayer appeared in the Latin Vulgate of the Holy Bible after the Second Book of Chronicles, and was also found in the Alexandrian manuscript of the Holy Bible preserved in the British Museum, and it also appeared in the Greek, Syriac, Armenian, Coptic and Ethiopic copies and all the copies taken from the Greek copy. It is a wonderful prayer of repentance that Manasseh offered to God after a long wicked life in which he led his people to the worship of idols and every evil. After it God allowed him to be taken captive to Babylon and thrown into prison, and in the humiliation of the fetters Manasseh returned to himself and offered this prayer. It is suitable for every person who repents of his sins, to encourage him and give him hope for a new life. We have given the text of the prayer, and its explanation follows.

Manasseh begins his prayer by contemplating the attributes of God and His greatness, because when a person knows God he feels His holiness and becomes small before Him, and thus he begins to feel the fear of God, which leads him to repentance. In this verse Manasseh sees in God three attributes:

1- Almighty: in whose hand is everything and under whose authority are all human souls, Manasseh among them, and this consequently leads him to submit before God and repent of his sins. No one can flee from God, because everything is uncovered and laid bare before Him, and indeed is under His authority, and He can give him life or end it.

2- Who is in heaven: for He is exalted above all material and earthly things, and before His exaltation the hideousness of sin appears, so a person hastens to repentance to be rid of it, and then he can stand and appear before God.

3- God of our fathers: Manasseh has boldness with God because He is the God of his fathers. Although He is the God of the fathers and their holy seed, He also loves all the seed from whom Manasseh came and desires their salvation, which gives hope to the sinner, so that he may come forward with repentance, asking for divine forgiveness.

The fourth attribute for which Manasseh glorifies God is that He is the Creator of everything, heaven and earth and all that is in them. He adorned heaven not only with the stars and planets but rather with the angels, and He adorned the earth not only with trees, plants and animals but above all with man, for whose sake He created everything. He loves him, and therefore rejoices in his repentance and his return to Him.
In this verse Manasseh sees three other new attributes in God, besides the four previous attributes, and they are:
5- He bound the sea:

Despite the greatness of the seas, which with their high waves can overturn the largest ships, God set for them a law, the law of the tides, by which the waves cannot cover the dry land; rather, when the water approaches the shore it returns again to the depths. The sea resembles a mighty man bound with chains; even if it moves toward the land and what is upon it, God stops it and returns it to its place. All this develops the fear of God within a person so that he repents.

6- He sealed the depths of the sea: Although man has gone down into the sea and learned much about it, he is still unable to reach all the depths of the seas, does not know the creatures that are in them, and cannot bear the conditions there. This shows the greatness of God's knowledge, of which man tries to discover something. So a person feels the weakness of his understanding before God and becomes very small, and all pride leaves him.
7- Everything trembles before Him:

If God moves the sea with His hand as though it were a small plaything, then everything in heaven and on earth is terrified before His power. When whirlwinds and hurricanes blow, they uproot huge trees and buildings before them and stir the seas so that they overflow onto the land. When the mountains move by earthquakes, and the icebergs by heat, and everything is terrified before the power of God, a person feels his weakness and at the same time trusts in the power of God that protects him, so he takes refuge in the arms of God with repentance and contrition.
In this verse he sees a new attribute in God, which is:

8- Unlimited: the glory of God that appears in nature in different forms surpasses the mind of man, and it is hard for him to know everything about it, which dazzles a person, so he humbles himself before God and keeps contemplating His beauty all the days, because He is unlimited.
And Manasseh sees a new attribute that concerns man directly, which is:

9- The wrath of His anger: the great, righteous and holy God is all light and is repelled by any evil; rather, He is greatly angry with sinners who persist in their evil, and this increases the fear of God in a person's heart, which pushes him to repentance.
Contemplate the attributes of God so that your heart is drawn to Him, and you praise Him and glorify Him, and this pushes you to purity and the rejection of every sin.

entries.section: (2) The God of those who repent

paragraphs.text: As he contemplates the attributes of God, Manasseh moves in his prayer to God's love for mankind, His mercy and His forgiveness of their sins, and he sees in Him the following:

1- His unlimited mercy: besides His justice, His wrath and His severe punishment of sinners who persist in their evils, He is also very merciful to all repentant sinners; indeed, His mercy cannot be counted. Whatever the sins of Manasseh and however wide his evils, the mercy of God is wider, because it is unlimited and forgives all the sins of the repentant.
2- Most High, merciful: although God is very high and exalted above all men, He is very tender, for He sees men as His children, so He forgives them their sins of which they repent.

3- Long-suffering: God was long-suffering toward Manasseh for decades of years and did not end his life, to give him an opportunity to repent, and finally, when he entered into affliction during his imprisonment in Babylon, he repented, so he obtained God's mercies in this prayer.

4- Righteous, and repenting of evil: God is holy, but He hates evil and does not desire the punishment of His children, because He "will have all men to be saved, and to come unto the knowledge of the truth" (1 Tim 2:4). God's repenting here of punishing the wicked means His turning back from punishing them when they repent, as He did with the people of Nineveh.

entries.section: (2) The God of those who repent

paragraphs.text: Then Manasseh sees a new attribute in God toward His repentant children, which is:
5- His goodness:
which appeared in His readiness to forgive all the sins of His children, and He set the way to that, which is repentance.

entries.section: (2) The God of those who repent

paragraphs.text: Finally Manasseh glorifies God, who receives the worst of sinners, and says to Him: Even though You ascribe Yourself to the righteous fathers Abraham, Isaac and Jacob because You are righteous and holy, yet when You set repentance You did not intend it for the righteous, but for wicked sinners like me, Manasseh, who did many evils before You.
How beautiful is repentance! It is the great way that carries the worst of sinners into the arms of God, so hasten to it whatever your sins, that you may enjoy His divine love.

With contrition Manasseh confesses that his sins are very many and were repeated in a way he cannot count, so that he says they are more than the number of the sand of the sea, and this shows two things:
1- Manasseh persisted for decades in spreading the worship of idols and all the lusts and evils that accompany it.
2- His intense regret for these sins and his feeling of the multitude of his sins.

Because of the multitude of his sins Manasseh feels deep contrition, so he looks to the earth, that is, to the dust from which he was taken, because Adam his father was created from the dust. And he feels he is not worthy to lift his eyes toward God in heaven. Although he longs for the pure heavenly life, in humility he declares that in himself he is unworthy of it. It is God who will grant him forgiveness as a free grace, so that he may be able to look at Him. His sense of regret is increased by the fact that he wronged many, not only by taking their rights but by causing them to stumble, because he led his people astray from the worship of God and encouraged them to idolatry and every evil in it (2 Kgs 21:9). His injustice reached those nearest to him, for he killed his son, offering him as a sacrifice to Molech and burning him with fire to please this pagan god (2 Kgs 21:6). In sum, he shed much blood unjustly (2 Kgs 21:16).

His sins make Manasseh bow his head toward the earth, not only because of the weight of the iron fetters with which his hands were bound, but even more because of the hideousness of his sins, which he carried on his back, so he bowed down to the earth weeping and broken, that God might not deprive him but forgive him.
I have angered Your wrath: I have stirred up Your intense anger against me and deserved every punishment.
My abominations: my defiled and filthy evils.

Manasseh declares his responsibility for stirring up God's anger against him because of the multitude of his sins. This made him troubled, having lost his peace and rest. And when Manasseh repented, he discovered that his sins were uncovered before God, and that in ignorance he had done all these evils in God's hands. Even though God had been long-suffering toward him, he deserved discipline and every punishment.

Manasseh also declares his responsibility for rejecting God's commandments and will, since he did the opposite, which are sins and all kinds of uncleanness and defilement. In defiance of God, Manasseh set up idols and pagan worship in every place of his kingdom, even before the Temple of God itself, and now he confesses that all these were very hideous sins.

If you offer repentance for your sins and show their hideousness, you draw God's mercies upon you and enjoy His mercy, but if you neglect repentance you bring God's wrath upon yourself, so take care to examine yourself every day, that you may sleep at peace in the hands of God.

entries.section: (4) Manasseh's humility and his asking for forgiveness

paragraphs.text: Be angry with me forever: that is, You would cast me into eternal torment as a punishment for my sins.

Finally, in humility which he expresses not only by bending his knees but the knees of his heart, that is, Manasseh is broken, and from this humility he looks to the goodness of God, asking forgiveness of his sins. He is unworthy because of the multitude of his sins, but his hope is in the mercy of God. As he confesses and affirms his sins and his knowledge of his evils, he implores God to forgive him all these sins and not to call him to account for them, or be angry with him and bear a grudge against him because of these evils, and so cast him into eternal destruction.

entries.section: (4) Manasseh's humility and his asking for forgiveness

paragraphs.text: Manasseh describes God with a beautiful attribute, that He is the God of those who repent. There is no person without sin, but there is one who returns by repentance, and he is one of the children of God, and there is one who insists on his sins, and he is one of the children of the devil.

entries.section: (4) Manasseh's humility and his asking for forgiveness

paragraphs.text: Manasseh begs God to show His goodness in him, that is, His mercy; for despite Manasseh's unworthiness he begs God to grant him forgiveness as a divine grace. And he hopes that God will give him of His goodness, that is, make Manasseh good.

entries.section: (4) Manasseh's humility and his asking for forgiveness

paragraphs.text: When Manasseh receives salvation from his many sins and forgiveness through the multitude of God's mercies, this pushes him to praise God and glorify Him all the days of his life. For the divine forgiveness of all these sins surpasses the mind, and Manasseh has nothing but thanksgiving and praise. This is the feeling of every truly repentant person before God.

entries.section: (4) Manasseh's humility and his asking for forgiveness

paragraphs.text: Thus Manasseh joins the angels, who are the powers and hosts of heaven, and praises God with them; that is, Manasseh does his natural work as a man, beginning with praise on earth, which is completed in heaven after his departure from this body.
It is clear that a person immersed in sin has no spiritual inclinations, so he does not love prayer and praise, but when his sins are released, his feelings are set free for prayer and praise.

Thank God every day after you confess your sins, because He receives you and forgives them to you, and awaits you in the sacraments of Confession and Communion, to complete His grace for you. Indeed, hold fast to your prayers and your praises every day, because they are your natural life and your delight.
The City of David: also called Mount Zion, located in the southeast of Jerusalem, and in it are the tombs of the kings of Judah.

Gihon: it is the Kidron Valley, which extends from the northeast of the city of Jerusalem to its south. The Fish Gate: one of the gates of Jerusalem, located in its north and beside the fish market, through which the fishermen enter with their fish.
Ophel: a fortified high place located east of Jerusalem, south of the Temple and north of the City of David, or Mount Zion.

After Manasseh's repentance he cared for the kingdom of Judah and began with Jerusalem, so he built a wall for it, extending from the north of the city at the Fish Gate and turning westward until it reached the south of the city, at the Kidron Valley. He also built a very high wall around Ophel, which is a very fortified place.
He also cared for the protection of the cities of Judah and placed in each of them one of the commanders of his army, with a large number of soldiers.

This signifies that the repentant person should fortify himself against the attacks of evil, and not be satisfied with rejecting sin but strengthen his relationship with God, so that the devil cannot attack him or overcome him.

Hold fast to your spiritual striving throughout your life, and do not be satisfied with leaving the difficult sins into which you have often fallen, but be constant in your relationship with God, growing in His fear and love.
The images: statues resembling the gods; it is said that Manasseh also made statues of himself resembling him, for them to worship.
The mountain of the house of the Lord: a hill located northeast of the city of Jerusalem, called Mount Moriah.

Among the important works that King Manasseh did after his repentance was removing the idols and the altars of the idols that he had built in Jerusalem, and even inside the two courts of the house of the Lord (v. 5), and he cast these statues outside Jerusalem, but unfortunately he did not break them or burn them, as other righteous kings did. Therefore, when his son Amon reigned after him, he took these statues and set them up again, worshipped them and sacrificed (v. 22).

Manasseh removed the pagan worship that he had set up in the days of his early reign, when he was far from God before he repented, a period of nearly fifty years; for he reigned fifty-five years, and he began to reign at the age of twelve and was taken captive at the age of fifty-eight (in the year 648 B.C.), as the ancient manuscripts indicate; that is, he repented in the last years of his life, after his return from Babylon.

After he repented, Manasseh cared not only about removing the pagan worship but also about calling his people to the worship of God; for he repaired the altar of God, which had been neglected for decades of years, then offered upon it peace offerings and thanksgiving to God, who accepted his repentance, and he encouraged his people, indeed commanded them to worship God as He commanded in His law.

Manasseh removed the temples of the idols and the statues, but time did not allow him to remove the high places on which they offered worship to the host of heaven. But Manasseh forbade offering any pagan worship upon them, so the people offered upon them the worship of God and sacrifices, though this was not right, because sacrifices should be offered only in the Temple of God; yet at least this worship was a return to God and a rejection of the idols.
The seers: plural of seer, a person who sees visions from God and prophesies and proclaims the voice of God to the people, and who wrote the visions, prophecies and instructions in a book.

As for the details of Manasseh's life, whether in the period of his evil conduct and his encouragement of the worship of idols by which he led the people astray from God, all of it is written in the acts of the kings of Israel and also the acts of the seers. In these books the seers' rebuke of Manasseh in the days of his departure from God is mentioned, and then these books contain his repentance and his return to God, then his prayer, which God answered, so He brought him back from Babylon, and he began his reforms in Jerusalem and Judea, as evidence of his repentance and his attempt to bring the people back to God, although only a few of them returned, because they had become fixed in the worship of idols and had forgotten God.

Manasseh died after he had reigned 55 years, at the age of 67, and it seems that he commanded that they bury him in the garden of his house, because he felt he was unworthy to be buried in the tombs of the kings, and this shows his humility and his deep repentance. Then his son Amon reigned after him.

entries.section: (4) The reign of Amon over Judah

paragraphs.text: After the death of Manasseh his son Amon reigned, and he was twenty-two years old, that is, a young man, and he was the fifteenth king on the throne of Judah. He walked in evil, offered sacrifices to the idols and departed from God, and did not learn from the repentance of his father, which took place when he entered into great affliction in his imprisonment in Babylon.

May you learn from the virtues of others and also from their mistakes, so that you try to acquire the virtues and keep away from the mistakes whose bitter end you have seen. Everything that happens around you is a personal message to you from God, that you may turn away from your sins and draw near to Him.

entries.section: (4) The reign of Amon over Judah

paragraphs.text: Amon continued in evil and the worship of idols and did not return from them by repentance to God like his father; perhaps he said, I will repent later, as my father repented, but I want to enjoy lusts now, and he forgot that he does not know the day of his end in this world. So he reigned only two years, and this was by God's arrangement, so that he would not increase his evils and draw his people further away from God.

Most likely the people continued in the worship of idols and did not repent with Manasseh, which helped Amon in the worship of idols, perhaps by the encouragement of his counselors and servants. In general, this shows us that the evil a person does causes others to stumble, and even if he repents he may not be able to bring back to God those whom he caused to stumble.

entries.section: (4) The reign of Amon over Judah

paragraphs.text: God ended the life of Amon two years after he became king, when he was twenty-four years old, for his servants rose up against him and killed him, and so his evil came upon his own head.

entries.section: (4) The reign of Amon over Judah

paragraphs.text: The people of the kingdom of Judah were enraged at the killers of the king, so they killed them. They buried Amon in the garden of his house, which is called the garden of Uzza (2 Kgs 21:26). Then they made his young child Josiah king after him. Josiah the righteous king
The Baals: that is, the altars of Baal, a well-known pagan god.
The images (poles): plural of a pole, a wooden pillar set up for the worship of foreign gods, whom they believed to be in heaven.
The molten images: the statues they cast for the pagan gods, that is, the idols they made from various metals.

Josiah reigned eight years, and when he was still a youth, after eight years, that is, when he reached the age of sixteen, and he was sixteen years old, his concern for the worship of God appeared, and he attached himself to Him with all his heart. Then twelve years after he ascended the throne, when he was twenty years old, he began his reforms. He first took care to remove the traces of idol worship from Jerusalem and all Judah, whether the idols, or the poles they had made for the worship of foreign gods, as well as the altars of the Baals that had been built on the high places for the worship of idols. So he destroyed everything connected with the foreign gods, such as the images of the sun that had been made for the worship of the sun, and he even beat them to pieces, then strewed them on the graves of the wicked who had worshipped these idols.

We notice here Josiah's early concern for the worship of God and for removing idol worship, from the time he was sixteen years old. Perhaps he benefited from the mistakes of his father and his grandfather, for his father Amon died young without repenting of his sins, and he died at the age of twenty-four, whereas his grandfather Manasseh repented in the last days of his life, when he was nearly sixty years old.

Josiah wanted to defile the pagan altars, so he burned the bones of the priests of the idols on them, so that no one could use them or their fragments. In this way he cleansed Jerusalem of every trace of idol worship. He was the first king to remove the altars from the high places, for the righteous kings who preceded him, from Solomon to Josiah, did not remove the pagan altars on the high places but made them for the Lord; yet the wicked kings returned and offered sacrifices to the idols on them. Therefore Josiah took care to remove and defile these altars on the high places, so that no traces would remain to help the wicked to worship on the high places. Although the kings who came after Josiah, that is, his sons, returned and worshipped idols and turned away from God. Thus the prophecy of the man of God was fulfilled, which he had spoken about three hundred years earlier, in the days of Jeroboam, the first king of Israel, that a king named Josiah would come and break down the pagan altars (1 Kgs 13:2). The people, who were immersed in the worship of idols, had forgotten the prophecies of God, but the word of God does not pass away.

Josiah was not content to cleanse his kingdom, that is, Jerusalem and Judah, but moved to remove idol worship in the other tribes, such as Manasseh, Ephraim, Simeon and Naphtali, and even all the ruins around the cities in which idol worship had been established. These tribes were no longer an independent kingdom, for the kingdom of Assyria had taken possession of them, so Josiah seized this opportunity and boldly advanced to cleanse his brethren in the rest of the tribes of their attachment to idols, in order to bring them back to the worship of the Lord. This shows the extent of his zeal for the Lord and his love for all the Jews; even those who had gone astray and turned away for a time from the worship of God, Josiah tried to bring back, so that they might be one people who believe in God and reject the worship of idols.

He was meticulous in removing everything connected with idols, whether the altars, or the poles, or the statues such as the images of the sun, and he even beat them to pieces so that no part of them could be used afterward for evil worship. And after he completed the cleansing of the tribes that were called the kingdom of Israel, he returned with joy to his capital, the holy city of Jerusalem.

Be meticulous in removing every trace of sin from your house, and also leave behind every evil thought and everything that could bring you back to evil. When God sees your care, He will remove your sins from you and let you enjoy fellowship with Him.

entries.section: (1) The Passover and the organization of the Temple

paragraphs.text: The author of the book announces that Josiah kept the Passover at its appointed time, the fourteenth day of the first month, and that this was in the eighteenth year of his reign, that is, when he was twenty-six years old. Josiah was able to keep the Passover at its appointed time because he had found the book of the Law and prepared for keeping the Passover, whereas King Hezekiah was not able to keep the Passover at its appointed time, so he kept it a month late. Therefore Josiah's Passover is considered greater, because he kept it with full preparation for it.

Josiah's concern for the Passover is considered a great work, because the Passover is the most important of the feasts of the Jews. Their life began with it when they went out of the land of Egypt and were freed from its bondage, and it is also the end of the Jewish feasts, since Christ kept the Passover for the last time on Holy Thursday, and after it He instituted the Lord's Supper, which is the sacrament of the Eucharist, to which the Passover pointed.

How good it is to prepare for every spiritual practice, so that you may feel it and enjoy God. Pray psalms as you go to church and pray at its door, so that you may feel the Divine Liturgy, and prepare yourself for prayer with a reading, or a prostration (metanoia), or a hymn, to help you concentrate on the words of the prayer. God rejoices in your care, and gives you comforts and warm feelings.

entries.section: (1) The Passover and the organization of the Temple

paragraphs.text: Their charges: their duties and responsibilities.

After Josiah restored the Temple, which had been neglected, he took care to encourage the priests, and distributed the work among them according to their responsibilities, each one in his place, whether in the service of offering the sacrifices on the bronze altar, or the laver, that is, the sea for washing, or the service of offering incense, or the lampstand, or the showbread, in addition to their examining the people who came forward to worship, so that they would be clean and free of leprosy. This was according to what he had learned from the Law of Moses and from all those who taught him, as will appear in the following verses; that is, he was meticulous and careful about everything he had received, so that he might do everything in a way that pleases God.

entries.section: (1) The Passover and the organization of the Temple

paragraphs.text: Josiah took care to establish the Levites in their work, meaning by them the priests and the Levites, because the priests are part of the tribe of Levi. He describes them here by two things, to stress to them their commitment to both:
1- Teaching the people the Law of God.
2- Taking care to sanctify themselves, so as to be an example to the people.
He also commanded the priests to return the ark of the covenant of God to its place in the Holy of Holies, since it had been removed from its place for one of these reasons:
1- Perhaps the wicked kings had removed the ark and put it in a side chamber in the Temple, because of their lack of concern for the worship of the Lord.

2- Perhaps the righteous priests in the days of the wicked kings had hidden the ark in one of the chambers of the Temple, so that the hands of the kings would not reach it to break it up and use the gold that was on it.
Josiah commanded the Levites to take care of the service of the Lord in His house, to help the people in worship, and to guide them in all the rites.

entries.section: (1) The Passover and the organization of the Temple

paragraphs.text: Josiah asked the Levites to arrange, through their chiefs, the service that fell to them according to their fathers' houses, that is, to divide themselves into courses, each course serving the house of the Lord for a week, according to what David taught, and then his son Solomon, who divided the Levites into twenty-four courses, each course serving the house for a week twice a year. These courses were for the priests and also for the Levites (1 Chr 24). This shows Josiah's meticulousness and his concern to organize the service of the Temple in the fullest way.

entries.section: (1) The Passover and the organization of the Temple

paragraphs.text: Josiah commanded the Levites to keep the Passover at its appointed time, and he also asked them to sanctify themselves and to sanctify their brethren from the rest of the tribes, and to teach them how to choose the Passover lamb according to what the Law prescribed, to slaughter the lamb for them, and to teach them how to eat it. For Josiah had divided the courses of the Levites among the tribes, so that each group of Levites would be responsible for a number of their brethren, so that everything would be done with order and care in this great feast, the feast of the Passover, as the verse indicated in (v. 5): "according to the divisions of the families of the fathers of your brethren the people, and after the division of the family of the Levites."

We notice Josiah's command to the Levites to sanctify themselves and to sanctify their brethren in preparation for keeping the Passover. Purity and cleanness are a necessity in the life of any servant before he begins his service, so that he cleanses his heart by repentance and prayer.

entries.section: (1) The Passover and the organization of the Temple

paragraphs.text: So that the Passover might be completed and none of the people might excuse himself because of his poverty, Josiah gave from his own property thirty thousand lambs and kids for keeping the Passover. In addition to that, he also gave three thousand bullocks, for the people to make into peace offerings, that they might rejoice with the Lord in gladness at this great feast. The king also gave kids, which were acceptable for keeping the Passover and which the poor offered because their price was lower than that of lambs (Ex 12:5). This shows two things by which Josiah was distinguished:
1- Josiah's generosity in giving.
2- His great concern that all the people keep the Passover and rejoice with God with peace offerings.

entries.section: (1) The Passover and the organization of the Temple

paragraphs.text: The chief priests who were in the house of the Lord followed the king's example, Josiah, in his giving for the feast of the Passover, so they too gave a large gift: two thousand six hundred lambs for keeping the Passover and three hundred bullocks for peace offerings.

entries.section: (1) The Passover and the organization of the Temple

paragraphs.text: The chiefs of the Levites also followed King Josiah's example, so they gave five thousand lambs for the Passover and five hundred bullocks for peace offerings. This shows the submission of the servants, that is, the priests and the Levites, to the king, their following his example, and their fear of God; that is, holiness had spread through the whole kingdom, and this of course gladdened God. If you compare the gifts that King Josiah and his chiefs gave (vv. 7-9) with what Hezekiah and his chiefs gave (ch. 30:24), you will notice that Josiah and his chiefs were more generous than Hezekiah. This shows Josiah's great concern and the favorable circumstances that helped this giving more than Hezekiah's straitened financial circumstances. Consequently, this Passover was the greatest Passover kept throughout the era of the kings.

entries.section: (1) The Passover and the organization of the Temple

paragraphs.text: With this great organization, the priests, the Levites and the people were prepared to keep the Passover. The priests slaughtered the animals and the Levites flayed their skins, and the priests sprinkled the blood on the bronze altar. This was a new rite which had not been done in the days of Moses in Egypt, since Moses had not yet received the Law and the system of sacrifices in full.

entries.section: (1) The Passover and the organization of the Temple

paragraphs.text: The priests removed the portions set apart for the sacrifice, to be offered to God on the bronze altar and burned on it (Lev 3:9), and then they gave the rest of the sacrifice for the people to roast and eat. They would slaughter and remove what was offered for the burnt offering, and then distribute the rest to the people according to their fathers' houses; that is, everything was done with precise order despite the vastness of the work. The priests also did this with the peace offerings from the bullocks, as they did with the Passover sacrifices. All this was according to what the Law of Moses prescribed.

entries.section: (1) The Passover and the organization of the Temple

paragraphs.text: The cauldrons: plural of cauldron, a large pot.
The dishes: plural of dish, which is a plate.

After the priests slaughtered the Passover and the Levites flayed it and gave it to the people, the people took it and roasted it, as the Law prescribed, although in the Hebrew original the word "roasted" and the word "boiled" in this verse are a single word, "bashal," which means to cook; that is, they cooked it, as is mentioned in (Deut 16:7). After that they boiled the peace offerings, which are the holy things, in pots, and put them in dishes for them to eat. Perhaps the Levites helped in the cooking and then gave to the people.

entries.section: (1) The Passover and the organization of the Temple

paragraphs.text: After the Levites made sure that the Passover had been prepared for all the people, they took care to prepare the Passover for the priests, that is, they cooked it for them, because the priests were busy offering up the portions of the sacrifices that were to be burned for God on the bronze altar. Finally, the Levites prepared the Passover for themselves and ate it.

Here the Levites' care appears, first for the people and then for themselves at the end. This is true love: that a person put the other before himself and arrange the needs of others before his own needs.

entries.section: (1) The Passover and the organization of the Temple

paragraphs.text: He adds here also that courses of the Levites carried out other works during the feast of the Passover, such as:
