1- The singers, that is, the Levites responsible for praise, under the leadership of the sons of Asaph, who praised throughout the period of the celebration of the feast of the Passover, according to what David had done when he appointed the chiefs of the singers, Asaph, Heman and Jeduthun, and all those who followed them from among their brethren the singers. So Josiah took care to complete the same order of praise.
2- The porters, who were responsible for guarding the gates of the Temple.

For all these courses, their brethren the Levites took care to prepare the Passover for them because of their being occupied with their service, so that in the end all might eat and rejoice together at the feast of the Passover.
From this appears Josiah's meticulousness in carrying out all the rites that had reached him, whether from the Law of Moses (vv. 6, 12, 13) or from his fathers David and Solomon (v. 4).

entries.section: (1) The Passover and the organization of the Temple

paragraphs.text: Thus Josiah completed the Passover and had everyone celebrate it, and then they celebrated the feast of unleavened bread after it, which lasted seven days. The Passover signifies the sacrifice of Christ on the Cross, and the unleavened bread, which is free of leaven, signifies the pure life, far from evil, which is lived by the person who belongs to Christ and receives his salvation through the Church and her sacraments.

We notice the importance of the service of the Levites, which includes the greatest works and the least, yet all are important because they are offered to God faithfully. They carried the ark of the covenant of God, and they also took care of flaying the animals, cooking them and putting them in dishes.

entries.section: (1) The Passover and the organization of the Temple

paragraphs.text: This Passover which Josiah completed in the eighteenth year of his reign was the greatest Passover kept throughout the period of the kings. None like it had been kept since the days of the judges, the last of whom was the prophet Samuel. All the people of the kingdom of Judah took part in it, as well as their brethren from the tribes who had obeyed God and responded to Josiah's call.

It appears from what has preceded in this chapter and the one before it that Josiah took care to cleanse and remove the idols, then to restore the house of the Lord, and God favored him with the discovery of His commandments, and then he moved to renew his covenant with God by keeping the Passover. Whoever cares to repent of his sins and to build his spiritual life, God reveals to him His knowledge, and he renews his covenant with God. This is accomplished through repentance and confession, Communion from the Holy Mysteries, care to read God's commandments and keep them in the Holy Bible, and care for spiritual edification, that is, for all the means of grace.
Necho: the Pharaoh of Egypt, called Necho II, of the twenty-sixth dynasty, who reigned in the period (610-595 BC). Carchemish: a city on the north of the Euphrates River, lying east of Aleppo.

After Josiah kept the Passover in the eighteenth year of his reign (v. 19), thirteen years passed in quiet, since Josiah reigned thirty-one years (ch. 34:1). During them Josiah continued to hold fast to the worship of the Lord, but his people in the kingdom of Judah were not wholehearted before God. This means that Josiah was not able to remove completely the effects of the corruption done by King Manasseh and after him his son Amon from the hearts of the people. Although Josiah removed idol worship, the people continued to love it, and perhaps kept some statues in their houses, as is proved by the following:
1- God did not allow the captivity in the days of Josiah because of his own humbling of himself and his returning to God.
2- God's wrath against His people remained, as mentioned in the words of the prophetess Huldah (ch. 34:22-28).

3- All the sons of Josiah walked in idol worship after him and the people were led by them; that is, their hearts were still attached to idols, and even the house of Josiah himself, that is, his sons, loved idols.

In the thirty-first year of Josiah's reign, when he was thirty-nine years old, he learned that Necho, king of Egypt, had moved with his army toward Carchemish, claiming that he would help Assyria against the strong countries around it, such as Media, Persia and Babylon. Josiah feared the return of strength to Assyria, because he had taken advantage of its weakness and had taken possession of some of the lands of the tribes that were subject to it, until he reached the plain of Jezreel and Samaria (2 Kgs 23:15-20). So he rose up to fight Necho and block him from reaching Carchemish. We notice here, in this situation, that despite Josiah's piety and his holding fast to the worship of God, he did not first ask God before this war, and this was a mistake that led to his death. Perhaps he did not ask God because of a spiritual coldness that came over him, though he continued to worship God, he and all his capital Jerusalem (2 Chr 34:33).
The valley of Megiddo: a plain beside Mount Tabor, lying on the main road between Egypt and Mesopotamia, that is, Iraq.

When Necho learned that Josiah had risen with his army to fight him, he sent to him to keep out of his way, and assured him that he did not wish to fight him and that God, the God of Pharaoh, to whom he had prayed, had not directed him to fight Josiah. Here we find a divine warning on the lips of this pagan man, Necho, to Josiah, so that he too might return to his God and ask Him whether he should fight Necho or not. For God wished to save Josiah to the last moment, but he rushed in to fight Necho and did not seek God. He drew up a battle plan and disguised himself as an ordinary soldier and did not wear his royal robes, perhaps thinking to protect himself by this, and forgetting that God alone protects His children. In this he fell into the same error as the wicked Ahab, who relied on his own mind alone and disguised himself, and was killed in the battle (2 Chr 18:29). This means that Necho's word to Josiah was a message from God to him, so that he might examine himself. There is also an opinion that the God of whom Necho spoke is the God of Israel, who perhaps appeared to Necho and encouraged him to fight Assyria; in this way, the meaning of Necho's word to Josiah would be that the God of Israel is the One who moved Necho against Assyria and not against Josiah.

God allowed King Josiah to be struck by an arrow in a dangerous place, so he was gravely wounded, perhaps the arrow struck him in his heart. So the king asked those with him to carry him to a second chariot, because he felt the seriousness of his condition, hoping that they might be able to treat him, or at least that they would not leave him in the hands of the enemies, lest they deal cruelly with him.

Josiah's servants quickly moved their king to his second chariot, which was traveling beside him, and hurried to take him out of the battle and returned with him to Jerusalem. There he died, and they buried him in the tombs of the kings with great honor. The people of Jerusalem and Judah gathered and wept for him and made a great mourning for him.

Thus Josiah died as God had told him through the prophetess Huldah, before he saw the ruin and destruction of Jerusalem and the land of Judah, because he was a devout man who humbled himself before God and kept His commandments (ch. 34:22-28).

All the great men took part in weeping for King Josiah, the righteous one, the like of whom had not arisen from the days of David nor afterward on the throne of Judah. The great prophet Jeremiah came forward and composed a lamentation for him (Jer 22:10, 11), and Jeremiah referred to him in his Lamentations (Lam 4:20). The singing men and singing women took part in lamenting Josiah, and for many years they continued to lament him, and they made it a necessity for all the singers to remember the great Josiah and lament him all the days. All this shows the extent of the people's love for him and their faith in his righteousness and piety.

The lamentations of Josiah were written in the book of lamentations, which is different from the book of the Lamentations of Jeremiah. Perhaps it was a book among the Jews in which they gathered the lamentations for great men.

The rest of the detailed events of Josiah's life, his love for his people, and his walking according to the law of the Lord from his childhood to the end of his life, all this was written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Israel and Judah, which is not one of the books of the Holy Bible, but a historical book.

Be careful all your life to seek God before every matter, small or great. Do not be content that you live in the Church and that you have sought God in some important matters of your life, but persevere in seeking God every day and before every work, however small it may seem.
Note: see the life of Josiah at the end of the book.
The last four kings of the kingdom of Judah

Nebuchadnezzar deposed King Jehoiachin, and made his uncle Mattaniah king in his place, and changed his name to Zedekiah. He was twenty-one years old at that time, so as to show his authority over the kingdom, and he reigned about eleven years, like Jehoiakim his brother. Jehoahaz and Jehoiakim also each reigned about three months, and perhaps God allowed Jehoahaz to reign three months so that Jehoiakim, who came after him, would be careful and walk with God and not imitate his brother who preceded him, lest he be deposed; but unfortunately he did not obey God and worship Him. The same thing was repeated afterward, and Jehoiakim was concerned that his son Jehoiachin should reign, and he even made him king with him during his life for ten years, then he reigned after the death of Jehoiakim for three months, and after that Nebuchadnezzar carried him captive to Babylon. Zedekiah was not deterred and did not walk with God, so his end, after about eleven years, was that he too was carried captive to Babylon.

If only you would learn from the mistakes of others, so that you avoid them and return to God and keep His commandments, and so deliver yourself from the snares of the demons, and enjoy God's care and love.

Zedekiah's rule was marked by turning away from God, encouraging idol worship, and the spread of injustice and evil lusts. And more than this, they mistreated the prophets of God whom He sent, especially the great prophet Jeremiah, who was strong in proclaiming the truth to every class of the kingdom, in addition to other prophets, such as Daniel, Ezekiel, Baruch, and the prophet Urijah, who was killed in the days of Jehoiakim (Jer 26:20-23). We see the care of God, who in times of extreme weakness sends great prophets, such as Jeremiah, Daniel and Ezekiel, to proclaim His voice with power.

Zedekiah was not content to walk in the way of evil, but also swore and pledged to Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, that he would submit to him, but he rebelled against him again (Ezek 17:18). Despite all of Jeremiah's warnings and admonitions, he was stubborn and refused to return to God by repentance.

As for the chief priests, the teachers, the leaders and all the people, they were influenced by Zedekiah's evil, so they worshipped idols and defiled the house of the Lord by abandoning His Law and walking against it, and so they provoked God to anger.

God's tenderness toward His people appears in His warning them and calling them to repentance, a long time before the punishment came, which was the captivity. He sent His messengers the prophets, not only immediately before the captivity, such as Jeremiah, Daniel, Ezekiel and Urijah, mentioned before in (v. 12), but He also sent earlier Elijah, Elisha, Isaiah and other prophets, that perhaps they would repent and He would forgive them.

But they neglected the word of God, and even insolently mistreated His prophets, not only by mocking them but even by killing them, such as Isaiah, whom they sawed with a wooden saw. Consequently, since no remedy availed with them, and there was no longer an opportunity for them to be healed of their spiritual diseases, He was finally compelled to punish them with captivity, so that some of them might return to Him in repentance, and He would forgive them.

Since the people rejected God's tenderness and compassion toward them (v. 15), He allowed the king of Babylon to discipline them, so he besieged Jerusalem, then attacked it and killed those in it and had compassion on no one, whether young man or young woman, old or young. He was cruel and destroyed everyone he met, and this was in the year 587 BC. This is the natural result of evil: whoever neglects the longsuffering of God must in the end face troubles and destruction.

The opportunity of a lifetime is offered to you by God, so that you may know Him and repent of your sins. If only you would seize it, to draw near to Him and enjoy His care on earth, and then fellowship with Him and the sight of His glory, which cannot be expressed, in heaven.

Nebuchadnezzar also gathered what remained of the vessels of the house of the Lord, whether the large ones, such as the bronze pillars, or the small ones, such as the gold vessels used in the Holy Place; he took everything of value. Nebuchadnezzar had taken some of the vessels in the first captivity, in the days of Jehoiakim in the year 605 BC (v. 7), then another part, the precious one, in the days of Jehoiachin in the year 597 BC (v. 10), and now, in the year 587 BC, in the third captivity, at the end of Zedekiah's reign, he takes what remained in the house of the Lord. He also seized the chiefs responsible for the Temple and took possession of all the treasures that were in the house of the Lord and in the house of the king, and sent all this to Babylon.

After Nebuchadnezzar's army took everything precious in the house of the Lord, they burned it and broke down the wall of Jerusalem, and they also burned the king's house and the palaces of the great men. Thus they destroyed Jerusalem in this third captivity. Four years after this, Nebuzaradan, the captain of the guard, came to Jerusalem and took a number of captives to Babylon, and this is the fourth and last Babylonian captivity (Jer 52:30).

He refers here to those taken captive in the third and fourth captivities, who were sent to Babylon and became slaves to Nebuchadnezzar for seventy years, until Babylon fell and the kingdom of Media and Persia reigned in its place.

Thus the prophecy of the prophet Jeremiah was fulfilled, that the Babylonian captivity would last seventy years, and this was the making up of the rest of the land, as the Law prescribed, for God commanded that they let the land rest in the seventh year and not sow it (Lev 25:4). But they neglected this for long periods, from the days of Joshua until the Babylonian captivity, and the period in which the land was neglected was about 490 years, during which they sowed the land in the seventh year, so that the number is 490 ÷ 7 = 70. Therefore God punished them by having the Chaldeans take possession of Jerusalem and Judah and destroy them, and cultivation in them was neglected, so the land rested by compulsion for seventy years, which is the length of the Babylonian captivity. God's people had also neglected everything connected with the seventh year, including the freeing of their brethren, the slaves whom they owned, so God allowed them all to be enslaved for seventy years, in repayment of the rights of their wronged brethren.
